species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male, tethered singing preparation
claim: Two-photon calcium imaging of the ventral nerve cord in tethered, singing males shows one neural population active during both pulse and sine song, and a larger population, which includes the first, active during pulse song. dPR1 neurons are active only during pulse song; TN1A neurons are active during both songs.
source_title: Activity of nested neural circuits drives different courtship songs in Drosophila
authors: Shiozaki HM, Wang K, Lillvis JL, Xu M, Dickson BJ, Stern DL

claim: Optogenetic activation of the descending neuron pIP10 produces both pulse and sine song, while activation of the descending neuron pMP2 produces pulse song but not sine song. Both project heavily into the wing neuropils of the nerve cord.
source_title: Activity of nested neural circuits drives different courtship songs in Drosophila
authors: Shiozaki HM, Wang K, Lillvis JL, Xu M, Dickson BJ, Stern DL

claim: Brain recordings show the same nested activation pattern in the two descending pathways needed for singing. The authors also recorded pIP10 calcium signals together with song sound (the signal combines left and right pIP10). Connectome analysis shows these two descending pathways feed structured input to VNC neurons, matching the activation patterns.
source_title: Activity of nested neural circuits drives different courtship songs in Drosophila (PMC full text)
authors: Shiozaki HM et al.

claim: The 2022 bioRxiv preprint of this work (titled 'Combinatorial circuit dynamics...') described two descending pathways with different roles: pIP10 is active for both songs, so it acts as a general 'sing' signal, and pMP2 is pulse-selective. The published 2024 Nature Neuroscience paper keeps this idea of distinct descending signals and calls the VNC activity pattern 'nested' instead of 'combinatorial.' The exact 'when vs. what' wording of the preprint is not verified.
source_title: Combinatorial circuit dynamics orchestrate flexible motor patterns in Drosophila
authors: Shiozaki HM et al. (preprint)

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male (MANC connectome for wiring)
claim: Silencing and activation screens identified eight fru- and/or dsx-expressing cell types (pIP10, pMP2, dPR1, dMS9, vMS12, TN1A, dMS2, vPR9), each needed for normal pulse song, sine song, or both. In the MANC connectome (wiring only, one male) they are densely interconnected and connected to wing motor neurons, forming two nested feed-forward pathways with reciprocal and feedback links. The larger pathway underlies pulse song, which the authors argue is the more complex and ancestral song type.
source_title: Nested neural circuits generate distinct acoustic signals during Drosophila courtship
authors: Lillvis JL, Wang K, Shiozaki HM, Xu M, Stern DL, Dickson BJ

claim: Song-type roles are not cleanly separated. Manipulating the 'pulse' neurons dMS9 and vMS12 also changed sine amplitude or frequency. Manipulating the 'sine' neurons TN1A and dMS2 also changed pulse features. pIP10 and vPR9 affected many features of both song types.
source_title: Nested neural circuits generate distinct acoustic signals during Drosophila courtship (PDF)
authors: Lillvis JL et al.

claim: In isolated males, optogenetic activation of dMS9, vMS12, vPR6 or vPR13 produced some sine song, but silencing any one of them did not noticeably reduce sine song. So, for sine song, vPR6 activation can evoke it, but vPR6 has not been shown to be needed for it. Its role in pulse song is a separate question.
source_title: Nested neural circuits generate distinct acoustic signals during Drosophila courtship
authors: Lillvis JL et al.

claim: Five classes of fruitless neurons trigger or make up the song. In the brain, P1 and the descending neuron pIP10 mediate the decision to sing and acting on it. In the thorax, dPR1, vPR6 and vMS11 are proposed parts of a pattern generator that times and shapes song pulses. P1, pIP10 and dPR1 are male-specific.
source_title: Neuronal Control of Drosophila Courtship Song
authors: von Philipsborn AC, Liu T, Yu JY, Masser C, Bidaye SS, Dickson BJ

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of fruitless-expressing neurons in the thoracic-abdominal ganglia (nerve cord) produces wing movement and sound in both sexes. It produces authentic song only in males, or in females made to express male fruitless. So a song-like motor program exists in females but lies dormant because the commands to start song are missing.
source_title: Sex-Specific Control and Tuning of the Pattern Generator for Courtship Song in Drosophila
authors: Clyne JD, Miesenbock G

claim: The male-specific, doublesex-expressing thoracic interneurons TN1A are needed specifically for sine song. They can drive the wing motor neuron hg1, which is not sex-specific and is also needed for sine song. doublesex acting in TN1A increases TN1A branch density where hg1 dendrites sit, which supports the TN1A-hg1 connection.
source_title: Doublesex Regulates the Connectivity of a Neural Circuit Controlling Drosophila Male Courtship Song
authors: Shirangi TR, Wong AM, Truman JW, Stern DL

claim: Calcium imaging of wing muscles during song shows the direct control muscles i1, hg1-4 and b3 are all strongly active during pulse song. Song and flight use different patterns of muscle activity from a shared set of muscles and motor neurons, and the flight command overrides song.
source_title: Multifunctional Wing Motor Control of Song and Flight
authors: O'Sullivan A, Lindsay T, Prudnikova A, Erdi B, Dickinson M, von Philipsborn AC

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male (sender) and female (receiver)
claim: Male D. melanogaster song has at least three modes, not two: fast pulse (Pfast), slow pulse (Pslow) and sine. Pfast is louder and more common when the male is far from the female. Activity of identified song premotor and motor neurons affects which mode is chosen, and the two pulse types affect female behavior differently.
source_title: Discovery of a New Song Mode in Drosophila Reveals Hidden Structure in the Sensory and Neural Drivers of Behavior
authors: Clemens J, Coen P, Roemschied FA, Pereira TD, Mazumder D, Aldarondo DE, Pacheco DA, Murthy M

claim: Male song patterning is not a fixed action pattern. Males use fast changes in visual and self-motion feedback cues (his own locomotion as well as the female's movement and their distance) to choose song moment by moment. The authors found the same relationship in the other Drosophila species they tested.
source_title: Dynamic sensory cues shape song structure in Drosophila
authors: Coen P, Clemens J, Weinstein AJ, Pacheco DA, Deng Y, Murthy M

claim: An unsupervised hidden-state model finds three hidden internal states in courting males. Each state maps female feedback cues onto song modes differently, and the model predicts moment-to-moment song choices. Activating a pair of neurons earlier described as song command neurons (likely pIP10) is enough to switch the male between states.
source_title: Unsupervised identification of the internal states that shape natural behavior
authors: Calhoun AJ, Pillow JW, Murthy M

claim: Males sing simple single-mode trains far from the female and complex pulse-sine alternations near her. VNC song circuits show mutual inhibition and rebound excitability between the nodes that drive the two modes. pC2 neurons drive pulse song directly via pIP10 (simple song from brief input) and also recruit persistent P1a activity and disinhibit the VNC rebound circuit, enabling complex bouts. Unverified here: whether this paper shows P1a being driven by taste cues from tapping.
source_title: Flexible circuit mechanisms for context-dependent song sequencing
authors: Roemschied FA, Pacheco DA, Aragon MJ, Ireland EC, Li X, Thieringer K, Pang R, Murthy M

claim: pC2l neurons in the central brain respond to both sound and visual cues. In males, activating a subset of them triggers pulse song right away, followed by sine song after activation ends, and pC2l is needed for normal singing. In females, the same type is needed for normal responses to male song.
source_title: Shared Song Detector Neurons in Drosophila Male and Female Brains Drive Sex-Specific Behaviors
authors: Deutsch D, Clemens J, Thiberge SY, Guan G, Murthy M

claim: Courting males produce both airborne song and substrate-borne vibration, mostly in different behavioural contexts. The brain neurons P1a and pC2l can drive both signals through separate premotor pathways with cell-type-specific dynamics. A circuit model with recurrence and mutual inhibition explains why vibration is limited to contexts, such as a close or stationary female, where it is likely to be effective. The exact male counts come from the paper's figures and were not verified here.
source_title: A neural circuit for context-dependent multimodal signaling in Drosophila
authors: Steinfath E, ... Clemens J

species: Drosophila melanogaster, male sender and optogenetically controlled female receiver
claim: Using real-time closed-loop optogenetics, the male's song was made to trigger backward walking in the female (activation of Moonwalker descending neurons), which perturbed her feedback. Males trained this way later changed the contexts in which they sang to new females. This is usage learning of an innate song.
source_title: Recent social experience alters song behavior in Drosophila
authors: Roemschied FA, Ireland EC, Calhoun AJ, Choi M, Ahmed OM, Murthy M

claim: Optogenetic or thermogenetic activation of P1 neurons in solitary males quickly triggers courtship song that can persist for minutes after stimulation ends (Inagaki et al. 2014; Bath et al. 2014). Hoopfer et al. 2015 show that P1 activation also drives a persistent state that increases inter-male aggression.
source_title: P1 interneurons promote a persistent internal state that enhances inter-male aggression in Drosophila
authors: Hoopfer ED, Jung Y, Inagaki HK, Rubin GM, Anderson DJ

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male, tethered virtual-reality courtship
claim: In tethered males courting a fictive female (a dot target in virtual reality), P1 neurons became strongly active at courtship onset, stayed elevated through a courtship bout, and returned to baseline whenever the male paused pursuit.
source_title: An arousal-gated visual circuit controls pursuit during Drosophila courtship (preprint of Nature 2021 'Sexual arousal gates visual processing during Drosophila courtship')
authors: Hindmarsh Sten T, Li R, Otopalik A, Ruta V

species: Drosophila melanogaster, one adult male (whole CNS, EM)
claim: The complete male central nervous system connectome contains about 166,700 fully proofread neurons across brain and nerve cord, annotated for fruitless and doublesex expression, with about 11,700 cell types. Compared with the female brain it has 8,069 matching types, 138 dimorphic types, 289 male-specific and 71 female-specific types. These counts are from the Cell summary; the preprint reported 262 sex-specific plus 114 dimorphic types.
source_title: Sexual dimorphism in the complete Drosophila male central nervous system connectome
authors: Berg S et al. (FlyEM/Janelia, Cambridge, Google)

species: Drosophila melanogaster, male vs female connectomes
claim: In the male CNS versus female brain connectome comparison (wiring only, one animal per sex), sex-specific and dimorphic cell types are concentrated in higher-order central brain regions, while sensory and motor neurons within the CNS are largely similar between sexes. Known exceptions include some sensory afferents. The authors interpret dimorphic neurons as routing shared sensory input into sex-specific behavioural circuits.
source_title: Sexual dimorphism in the complete Drosophila male central nervous system connectome
authors: Berg S et al.

claim: The Janelia release highlights male pC1 neurons, a diverse dsx+ population (some also fru+) that includes the male-specific P1 subtypes, as promoting courtship song and aggression, based on earlier causal studies. pC1 neurons also exist in females, with different subtypes and roles, and the connectome itself is wiring only.
source_title: Researchers reveal connectome of the male fruit fly central nervous system
authors: Janelia Research Campus news

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male nerve cord (EM)
claim: In the MANC connectome (Cheong et al., eLife 2024), circuits from descending neurons to premotor and motor neurons were systematically mapped, and courtship-linked VNC types including TN1a, dPR1, vPR9 and vMS11 were identified. How older driver-line names (e.g., vPR6) map onto MANC types is not fully settled in the sources seen.
source_title: Organization of circuits linking descending input to motor output in the Drosophila Male Adult Nerve Cord connectome
authors: Cheong HSJ et al.
venue: eLife (reviewed preprint 2024; version of record reported 2026)

species: Drosophila melanogaster, male and female VNC connectomes
claim: A 2026 preprint aligns connectomes using network structure alone. It uses two complete male VNC connectomes as references to assign cell types to about 13,000 female VNC neurons, flag sex-specific and dimorphic types, and study female counterparts of the male song-production circuit.
source_title: Uncovering Sex Differences in the Drosophila Ventral Nerve Cord Through Connectome Alignment
authors: (authors not captured in search results)

species: Drosophila melanogaster and D. yakuba, adult males
claim: The homologous male-specific descending neuron pIP10 (one per hemisphere) was genetically targeted in D. melanogaster and D. yakuba. Its activation gave different song types in the two species: sine in D. melanogaster at low activation, 'clack' song in D. yakuba, and more pulse in D. yakuba at higher activation. The evolutionary change was placed downstream of pIP10's own physiology.
source_title: Neural Evolution of Context-Dependent Fly Song
authors: Ding Y, Lillvis JL, Cande J, Berman GJ, Arthur BJ, Long X, Xu M, Dickson BJ, Stern DL

species: Drosophila yakuba vs D. melanogaster, adult males
claim: D. yakuba, which lost sine song, lacks a TN1A-equivalent cell type. Its TN1 neurons can still drive the singing wing posture but not sine song. A divergent doublesex function in D. yakuba reduces TN1 number by promoting cell death.
source_title: Changes in the cellular makeup of motor patterning circuits drive courtship song evolution in Drosophila
authors: Ye D, Walsh JT, Junker IP, Ding Y

claim: Activating doublesex-expressing neurons in the female brain, with the pC1 cluster identified as critical, makes females court like males: mainly orienting and following, with occasional tapping and one-wing extension. Audio recordings show male-like song features, including sine and pulse episodes. The female brain therefore contains latent circuitry for male-like courtship and song.
source_title: Brain wiring explains sex differences in Drosophila behaviour (JEB summary of Rezaval et al. 2016)
authors: Rezaval C et al. (2016), summarized in Journal of Experimental Biology
venue: Journal of Experimental Biology (secondary summary); primary paper Current Biology 2016

claim: D. melanogaster females produce a copulation song by wing vibration during mating. It differs from male courtship song, requires DoublesexF-expressing neurons, and is modulated by seminal fluid from the male. A downstream effect on remating is not verified here.
source_title: Female copulation song is modulated by seminal fluid
authors: Kerwin P, Yuan J, von Philipsborn AC

claim: Hearing regulates male-male aggression, and courtship song and aggression song affect aggression differently. Males therefore have an acoustic threat or agonistic signal, but the neurons that produce aggression song were not identified in this work.
source_title: Hearing regulates Drosophila aggression
authors: Versteven M, Vanden Broeck L, Geurten B, Zwarts L, Decraecker L, Beelen M, Gopfert MC, Heinrich R, Callaerts P

species: Drosophila melanogaster, head-fixed adults, both sexes compared (pan-neuronal GCaMP)
claim: Volumetric pan-neuronal calcium imaging registered across the whole central brain found auditory activity in most central brain regions, including in neurons responsive to other modalities; responses were temporally diverse but the majority were tuned to courtship-song features.
source_title: Auditory activity is diverse and widespread throughout the central brain of Drosophila
authors: Pacheco DA, Thiberge SY, Pnevmatikakis E, Murthy M

claim: In the same whole-brain dataset, auditory responses were stereotyped across trials and animals in early mechanosensory regions and became more variable at higher stages of the putative pathway; this variability was largely independent of spontaneous movements.
source_title: Auditory activity is diverse and widespread throughout the central brain of Drosophila
authors: Pacheco DA, Thiberge SY, Pnevmatikakis E, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster (calcium imaging of JON subgroups)
claim: Johnston's organ neurons form five subgroups (JO-A to JO-E). Calcium imaging showed JO-A and JO-B are activated by antennal vibration (sound), while JO-C and JO-E respond most strongly to static antennal deflection. Silencing the A/B neurons impaired hearing (song responses) and silencing the C/E neurons impaired gravitaxis. Only the sound-sensitive neurons express the candidate mechanotransducer channel NompC, and the two subsets project to separate central pathways. (A proposed ~100 Hz frequency split between JO-B and JO-A still needs a primary source.)
source_title: The neural basis of Drosophila gravity-sensing and hearing
authors: Kamikouchi A, Inagaki HK, Effertz T, Hendrich O, Fiala A, Goepfert MC, Ito K

claim: Drosophila auditory receptor neurons adapt to stimulus mean and intensity, change their frequency tuning with sound intensity, and apply a quadratic nonlinearity, which together give an efficient representation of courtship song.
source_title: Quadratic and adaptive computations yield an efficient representation of song in Drosophila auditory receptor neurons
authors: Clemens J, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster (in vivo whole-cell patch clamp)
claim: Two cell types postsynaptic to antennal vibration receptors (A2 and B1) encode vibration differently. A2 cells receive excitation for both directions of antennal movement (twice per cycle) and their membrane low-pass filters it, so A2 tracks the vibration envelope. B1 cells are phase-sensitive (excited by forward or backward movement only) and band-pass filter oscillatory synaptic input at the stimulus frequency. Different B1 cells prefer different frequencies because of differences in voltage-gated Na+/K+ conductances.
source_title: Active Mechanisms of Vibration Encoding and Frequency Filtering in Central Mechanosensory Neurons
authors: Azevedo AW, Wilson RI

species: Drosophila melanogaster, males and females (neuronal inactivation/hyperactivation during behavior)
claim: Of seven auditory projection neuron types (aPNs) and five local interneuron types (aLNs) of the ascending mechanosensory pathway, only aPN1 (= AMMC-B1) and the GABAergic interneuron aLN(al) were necessary for behavioral song responses, in both males and females.
source_title: Neural pathways for the detection and discrimination of conspecific song in D. melanogaster
authors: Vaughan AG, Zhou C, Manoli DS, Baker BS

species: Drosophila melanogaster, females (calcium imaging/electrophysiology plus behavior)
claim: AMMC-B1 neurons show inter-pulse-interval (IPI) selectivity that differs from upstream JONs. Two GABAergic AMMC local interneurons receive auditory input and provide feedforward inhibition onto B1 neurons, and are proposed to shape B1 interval selectivity and the female response to song.
source_title: GABAergic Local Interneurons Shape Female Fruit Fly Response to Mating Songs
authors: Yamada D, Ishimoto H, Li X, Kohashi T, Ishikawa Y, Kamikouchi A

species: Drosophila melanogaster (calcium imaging of identified cell types)
claim: Calcium imaging of newly identified intermediate-layer auditory cell types (WED/VLP), together with known types such as B1 and pC2, showed a continuum of preferences between sine and pulse song modes rather than two separate channels. The '24' count comes from the researcher's source and was not independently confirmed.
source_title: Neural network organization for courtship-song feature detection in Drosophila
authors: Baker CA, McKellar C, Pang R, Nern A, Dorkenwald S, Pacheco DA, et al., Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult female (FlyWire/FAFB) with imaging cross-check
claim: Mapping synapses among these auditory cell types in FlyWire (adult female FAFB EM) showed that neurons with different song-mode preferences and response timescales are highly interconnected in a network without hierarchical structure. The authors call this the first circuit-level map of the fly auditory pathway and relate it to the imaged tuning. Synapse sign comes from predicted neurotransmitter identity (Eckstein/Funke classifier), not measured physiology.
source_title: Neural network organization for courtship-song feature detection in Drosophila
authors: Baker CA, McKellar C, Pang R, Nern A, Dorkenwald S, Pacheco DA, et al., Murthy M

claim: Zhou et al. 2015 used calcium imaging to show that in males, third-order vPN1 neurons prefer pulse song with long IPIs, and fourth-order pC1 responses across IPIs match the IPI tuning of song-induced male chaining. They proposed aPN1 -> vPN1 -> pC1 as the pathway. The 2026 male CNS connectome refines this: vPN1 is GABAergic, so its apparent excitation of pC1 is best explained by disinhibition (vPN1 inhibits the male-specific mAL, which inhibits pC1), not a direct excitatory link.
source_title: Central neural circuitry mediating courtship song perception in male Drosophila
authors: Zhou C, Franconville R, Vaughan AG, Robinett CC, Jayaraman V, Baker BS

claim: Genetic inactivation of vPN1 or pC1 disrupts song-induced male chaining (male-male courtship in response to song playback).
source_title: Central neural circuitry mediating courtship song perception in male Drosophila
authors: Zhou C, Franconville R, Vaughan AG, Robinett CC, Jayaraman V, Baker BS

species: Drosophila melanogaster, males and females (calcium imaging)
claim: Dsx+ pC2 neurons are tuned for multiple temporal features of pulse song, and song feature tuning is similar in male and female brains. The authors conclude that sex-shared song detectors drive divergent behaviors.
source_title: Shared Song Detector Neurons in Drosophila Male and Female Brains Drive Sex-Specific Behaviors
authors: Deutsch D, Clemens J, Thiberge SY, Guan G, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster, males and females (optogenetic/genetic silencing and activation)
claim: pC2l neurons in both sexes respond selectively to features of pulse song. Silencing pC2l in females reduces female slowing to pulse song. In males, optogenetic activation of a subset of pC2l acutely elicits pulse song, followed by transient sine song after the light goes off. Males with a subset of pC2l silenced still sang pulse song with normal IPIs, pulse shapes and carrier frequencies, but sang about twice as much as controls, mainly more sine song.
source_title: Shared Song Detector Neurons in Drosophila Male and Female Brains Drive Sex-Specific Behaviors
authors: Deutsch D, Clemens J, Thiberge SY, Guan G, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster, females (imaging, optogenetics, EM connectivity)
claim: Female vaginal plate opening (VPO, the acceptance act) is controlled by a pair of female-specific descending neurons (vpoDNs). vpoDNs receive excitatory input from auditory vpoEN neurons, which are tuned to features of D. melanogaster song, and from pC1 neurons, which encode mating status. The synaptic connections were confirmed in EM connectome data.
source_title: Neural circuit mechanisms of sexual receptivity in Drosophila females
authors: Wang F, Wang K, et al., Dickson BJ

species: Drosophila melanogaster, virgin vs mated females (calcium imaging)
claim: After mating, vpoDN song responses are attenuated but vpoEN responses are not, and pC1 neurons mediate this change. For vaginal plate opening, the key mating-status gate therefore sits where vpoDN integrates song and state. That does not exclude state-dependent modulation elsewhere in the auditory pathway.
source_title: Neural circuit mechanisms of sexual receptivity in Drosophila females
authors: Wang F, Wang K, et al., Dickson BJ

species: Drosophila melanogaster, females (thermogenetic/optogenetic manipulation plus calcium imaging)
claim: Activating pC1 or pCd neurons in females promotes receptivity and silencing them makes females unreceptive. Female pC1 neurons respond both to courtship song and to the male pheromone cVA, consistent with multisensory integration of courtship cues.
source_title: Central brain neurons expressing doublesex regulate female receptivity in Drosophila
authors: Zhou C, Pan Y, Robinett CC, Meissner GW, Baker BS

species: Drosophila melanogaster, females (optogenetics plus FAFB EM reconstruction)
claim: A subset of female Dsx+ pC1 neurons (pC1d/e) can drive minutes-long changes in female behavior in the presence of males. EM reconstruction of all their inputs and outputs revealed strong recurrent connectivity between pC1d/e and Fruitless+ aIPg neurons.
source_title: The neural basis for a persistent internal state in Drosophila females
authors: Deutsch D, Pacheco D, Encarnacion-Rivera L, et al., Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster, females (calcium imaging, optogenetics, EM connectivity)
claim: DNp13 descending neurons are command-type neurons for ovipositor extrusion (OE). They respond to male song through direct synaptic input from pC2l auditory neurons. Mating status does not change DNp13 song responses; it changes how effectively they engage OE motor circuits, via ppk+ uterine sensory neurons activated by ovulation.
source_title: Circuit and Behavioral Mechanisms of Sexual Rejection by Drosophila Females
authors: Wang F, Wang K, et al., Dickson BJ

species: Drosophila melanogaster, virgin vs mated females
claim: Male song is more likely to evoke vaginal plate opening in virgin females and ovipositor extrusion in recently mated females (Wang et al. 2020). The role of OE is disputed: Wang et al. treat it as a rejection behavior in mated females, while the companion paper by Mezzera et al. 2020 reports that OE promotes copulation attempts and signals acceptance in virgins.
source_title: Circuit and Behavioral Mechanisms of Sexual Rejection by Drosophila Females
authors: Wang F, Wang K, et al., Dickson BJ

species: Drosophila melanogaster, females and responding males
claim: Ovipositor extrusion is shown only by sexually mature females, only during courtship, and in response to male song. OE promotes male copulation attempts in both virgin and mated females and signals acceptance in virgins.
source_title: Ovipositor Extrusion Promotes the Transition from Courtship to Copulation and Signals Female Acceptance in Drosophila melanogaster
authors: Mezzera C, Brotas M, Gaspar M, Pavlou HJ, Goodwin SF, Vasconcelos ML

species: Drosophila melanogaster, unmated vs mated females aged 5-7 days (calcium imaging, RNAi, behavior)
claim: A 2025 iScience study (Kamikouchi-lab/Nagoya) reports that female JONs express several dopamine receptor types. Connectome data suggest some JONs contact dopaminergic neurons directly (wiring evidence). Dop1R2 knockdown in JONs reduced JON sound responses in unmated but not mated females (calcium imaging). Overexpressing Dop1R2 in JONs enhanced unmated females' song-response behavior in the lab's playback assay.
source_title: Mating status-dependent dopaminergic modulation of auditory sensory neurons in Drosophila
authors: Yamakoshi H, Horigome M, Yamamoto S, et al. (Nagoya University)

species: Drosophila melanogaster, freely courting pairs plus neural recordings
claim: During natural courtship, females are sensitive to long-timescale song structure (tens of seconds) and integrate song information. Simple computations applied to single-neuron responses can predict female locomotor behavior.
source_title: Connecting Neural Codes with Behavior in the Auditory System of Drosophila
authors: Clemens J, Girardin CC, Coen P, Guan XJ, Dickson BJ, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster, females (model fit to recorded neural data and courtship behavior)
claim: Comparing computational models of female song processing against neural activity and unrestrained courtship behavior, the best model used neurons that adapt to and accumulate their inputs, with heterogeneous nonlinear adaptation and slow integration. This let fine-scale song information persist in the population code for long periods.
source_title: Inferring neural population codes for Drosophila acoustic communication
authors: Pang R, Baker CA, Murthy M, Pillow J

species: Drosophila melanogaster, females (RNAi plus connectome analysis)
claim: A 2024 iScience study from the Kamikouchi lab with Janelia co-authors (likely Imoto K, ..., Aso Y, Funke J, ..., Kamikouchi A; confirm) reports the following. Song preference learning (reduced response to heterospecific song after hearing conspecific song) requires GABA made in pCd-2 neurons, a small Dsx+ population of about four cells per hemibrain. Female connectome data show direct, often reciprocal, pCd-2-pC1 connections. The sex used for the behavioral experiments, and the dopamine requirement, need confirming from the paper.
source_title: Neural-circuit basis of song preference learning in fruit flies
authors: Kamikouchi lab (Nagoya) with Janelia co-authors; full author list not confirmed in results

species: D. melanogaster vs D. simulans females (behavior plus neuroanatomy)
claim: D. melanogaster and D. simulans females each increase receptivity to songs with conspecific temporal patterns. JONs and AMMC-B1 neurons share morphology and neurotransmitters across the two species, and the early auditory circuit is largely conserved. AMMC-B1 temporal-pattern preferences are relatively similar across species, with slight but significant band-pass differences too small to explain the behavioral difference in song preference. The divergence in preference therefore likely lies downstream of B1.
source_title: Evolutionary conservation and diversification of auditory neural circuits that process courtship songs in Drosophila
authors: Kamikouchi lab (Nagoya); first author not confirmed in results

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male CNS compared with female connectomes
claim: The complete male CNS connectome (Cell 2026; preprint 2025, reportedly Berg, Beckett, Costa, Schlegel et al. with Janelia FlyEM, Cambridge/MRC LMB and Google) reports that sex-specific and dimorphic neuron types concentrate in higher brain centres, while the sensory and motor periphery is largely isomorphic. Cell-type counts should be taken from the final published version only.
source_title: Sexual dimorphism in the complete Drosophila male central nervous system connectome
authors: Janelia FlyEM, MRC LMB, University of Cambridge and Google Research consortium

species: Drosophila melanogaster, male CNS vs female (FlyWire) connectomes
claim: A male-female connectome comparison finds that vpoEN neurons have a strong sex-shared downstream partner (DNp55) and sex-specific partners (vpoDN in females, pC1_6a in males). This suggests the same auditory neuron type connects to different targets in each sex. Whether song activity actually flows this way in males has not been recorded.
source_title: Sexual dimorphism in the complete Drosophila male central nervous system connectome
authors: Janelia FlyEM, MRC LMB, Cambridge and Google Research consortium

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male (brain plus VNC connectome)
claim: The male CNS connectome identifies male-specific ascending neurons that carry information from nerve-cord song-generating neurons to brain song-detection circuits. The authors infer a closed loop in which the motor output of singing likely influences auditory detection of song.
source_title: Sexual dimorphism in the complete Drosophila male central nervous system connectome
authors: Janelia FlyEM, MRC LMB, Cambridge and Google Research consortium

claim: A 2025 annotation of the female FlyWire brain connectome identified putative Fruitless and Doublesex neuron types by matching morphology to light-microscopy data (reported counts: 1,278 Fru, 50 Dsx, 79 ambiguous; unverified) and characterized their connectivity. SAG ascending neurons relaying post-mating (sex-peptide) information to pC1 was established earlier by functional work (Feng et al. 2014 Neuron; Wang F et al. 2020 Nature).
source_title: Sexually-dimorphic neurons in the Drosophila whole-brain connectome
authors: not confirmed in results

species: Drosophila melanogaster (biophysical measurement of antenna and song amplitude in courting pairs)
claim: Laser Doppler vibrometry and acoustic measurements (likely Morley, Jonsson & Robert 2018, J Acoust Soc Am; confirm) report that the D. melanogaster antenna's mechanics are nonlinear. It is tuned near song frequencies at low amplitudes, and its resonance shifts up by hundreds of Hz at higher amplitudes. Song measured at the female during courtship was often louder than predicted, so under natural conditions the antenna may be operating outside its amplified, song-tuned regime.
source_title: Auditory sensitivity, spatial dynamics, and amplitude of courtship song in Drosophila melanogaster
authors: not confirmed in results

claim: Female D. melanogaster respond to amplitude modulation within courtship song and prefer their own strain's song amplitude envelope over a flat or a steeper gain profile.
source_title: Female Drosophila melanogaster respond to song-amplitude modulations
authors: not confirmed in results

claim: Or67d ORNs (DA1 glomerulus) are required for the acute behavioral responses to cVA. Without Or67d, males court other males more and females are less receptive. Or65a ORNs, a second cVA-sensitive class, were later shown to carry the effects of long-term cVA exposure, so 'single class' applies only to acute responses.
source_title: A single class of olfactory neurons mediates behavioural responses to a Drosophila sex pheromone
authors: Kurtovic A, Widmer A, Dickson BJ

claim: Or67d ORNs and DA1 PNs respond to cVA similarly in males and females (electrophysiology). However, the axon arbors of DA1 PNs in the lateral horn are sexually dimorphic and depend on fruitless (light-microscopy anatomy). This suggests the dimorphism lies in how DA1 PNs connect to third-order lateral horn neurons, not in how sensory neurons or PNs respond. Evidence type: anatomy (not a connectome) plus activity recordings that showed no sex difference.
source_title: The Drosophila pheromone cVA activates a sexually dimorphic neural circuit
authors: Datta SR, Vasconcelos ML, Ruta V, Luo S, Wong A, Demir E, Flores J, Balonze K, Dickson BJ, Axel R

claim: In males, a four-step cVA pathway was traced and recorded: Or67d ORN -> DA1 PN -> fru+ DC1 lateral horn neuron -> fru+ DN1 descending neuron. Electrophysiological recordings showed that DN1 responds to cVA, linking pheromone input to descending motor output.
source_title: A dimorphic pheromone circuit in Drosophila from sensory input to descending output
authors: Ruta V, Datta SR, Vasconcelos ML, Freeland J, Looger LL, Axel R

claim: cVA signals are sent to different sexually dimorphic lateral horn neuron classes in males and females (the aSP-f and aSP-g classes) through a fruitless-dependent 'bidirectional circuit switch'. In vivo whole-cell recordings combined with optogenetic stimulation of DA1 PNs showed sex-specific functional connectivity.
source_title: A bidirectional circuit switch reroutes pheromone signals in male and female brains
authors: Kohl J, Ostrovsky AD, Frechter S, Jefferis GSXE

claim: Acute cVA exposure promotes male-male aggression through Or67d ORNs (Wang & Anderson 2010). Long-term exposure from group housing instead reduces aggression through Or65a ORNs (Liu et al. 2011). The same pheromone can therefore push aggression either way depending on timescale, while also suppressing male-male courtship.
source_title: Identification of an aggression-promoting pheromone and its receptor neurons in Drosophila
authors: Wang L, Anderson DJ

claim: Combining the hemibrain/FlyWire connectomes with physiology, cVA processing splits in the lateral horn into parallel pathways. These represent the identity of the pheromone source and its position relative to the receiving fly.
source_title: Generating parallel representations of position and identity in the olfactory system
authors: Taisz I, Dona E, Munch D, ... Jefferis GSXE, Galili DS

claim: Foreleg ppk23+ gustatory neurons come in two functional subtypes. 'F-cells' respond to the female pheromone 7,11-HD and 'M-cells' respond to male pheromones (e.g., 7-T), as shown by calcium imaging. ppk23 neurons are needed for normal male courtship of females and for male-male courtship repulsion.
source_title: Contact chemoreceptors mediate male-male repulsion and male-female attraction during Drosophila courtship
authors: Thistle R, Cameron P, Ghorayshi A, Dennison L, Scott K (also Toda H, Zhao X, Dickson BJ 2012 Cell Reports; Lu B et al. 2012 PLoS Genet)

claim: Calcium imaging of P1 in males during foreleg pheromone stimulation shows that female contact pheromones excite P1 and the male pheromone 7-T inhibits it, a balance that biases mate choice (Kallman et al. 2015). Kallman et al. identified PPN1 relay neurons, and Clowney et al. 2015 identified vAB3 excitation and mAL inhibition. Exactly how 7-T -> PPN1 -> mAL -> P1 connect needs to be confirmed from the primary paper.
source_title: Excitation and inhibition onto central courtship neurons biases Drosophila mate choice
authors: Kallman BR, Kim H, Scott K

claim: P1 neurons act as a multisensory integrator in the male brain. They are excited by female contact pheromones via vAB3 and gated by feedforward inhibition via mAL, and the volatile pheromone cVA suppresses P1 excitation. This was shown with calcium imaging and electrophysiology in ex vivo and in vivo preparations with foreleg stimulation.
source_title: Multimodal chemosensory circuits controlling male courtship in Drosophila
authors: Clowney EJ, Iguchi S, Bussell JJ, Scheer E, Ruta V

claim: In males, dTrpA1 activation of fruitless-expressing neurons induced courtship acts, and courtship initiation correlated with activation of P1 interneurons, descending P2b neurons, or both (mosaic analysis). Female contact evoked activity in P1 in tethered males.
source_title: Female contact activates male-specific interneurons that trigger stereotypic courtship behavior in Drosophila
authors: Kohatsu S, Koganezawa M, Yamamoto D

species: Drosophila melanogaster vs D. simulans, males
claim: In D. simulans, 7,11-HD (a female pheromone of D. melanogaster) suppresses male courtship. Peripheral detection by ppk23+ neurons is conserved, but the central route to P1 differs. In D. melanogaster, 7,11-HD excites P1 via vAB3. In D. simulans, the balance shifts toward inhibition via the GABAergic mAL pathway, so P1 is not activated. This was shown by calcium imaging in both species. Whether PPN1 is part of the altered pathway is unconfirmed.
source_title: Evolution of a central neural circuit underlies Drosophila mate preferences
authors: Seeholzer LF, Seppo M, Stern DL, Ruta V

claim: Gr32a-expressing gustatory neurons are required for 7-T to promote male aggression and for normal suppression of male-male courtship. Whether Gr32a neurons themselves detect 7-T is disputed, since ppk23+ M cells also respond to 7-T. Contact chemosensation still sits upstream of the fight-or-court decision.
source_title: Hierarchical chemosensory regulation of male-male social interactions in Drosophila
authors: Wang L, Han X, Mehren J, Hiroi M, Billeter JC, Miyamoto T, Amrein H, Levine JD, Anderson DJ (see also Miyamoto T, Amrein H 2008 Nat Neurosci)

claim: LC10a lobula columnar visual projection neurons are needed for a courting male to track the female and to orient his unilateral wing extension toward her. Silencing LC10a impairs visual pursuit during courtship.
source_title: Visual projection neurons mediating directed courtship in Drosophila
authors: Ribeiro IMA, Drews M, Bahl A, Machacek C, Borst A, Dickson BJ

claim: Sexual arousal (P1 activity) gates visual processing during courtship. With two-photon imaging in tethered males pursuing a visual target, visual signals from the LC10a pathway drove pursuit only when males were aroused, and optogenetic P1 activation made males pursue a moving target.
source_title: Sexual arousal gates visual processing during Drosophila courtship
authors: Hindmarsh Sten T, Li R, Otopalik A, Ruta V

claim: A deep network trained with 'knockout training' on male courtship behavior mapped model units onto LC visual projection neuron types. It predicted that female features (position, size, heading) are carried by a combinatorial population code across many LC types, not by single dedicated channels. The prediction was tested against LC neuron imaging.
source_title: Mapping model units to visual neurons reveals population code for social behaviour
authors: Cowley BR, Calhoun AJ, Rangarajan N, ... Pillow JW, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster, male sender / female receiver
claim: Courting males make abdominal quivering movements that send substrate-borne vibrations. Females respond by becoming immobile (stopping), which helps copulation. Playing artificial vibrations reproduces the female stopping response.
source_title: Substrate-borne vibratory communication during courtship in Drosophila melanogaster
authors: Fabre CCG, Hedwig B, Conduit G, Lawrence PA, Goodwin SF, Casal J

claim: In virgin females, dsx+ pC1 neurons respond to cVA and courtship song in calcium imaging, and their activity bidirectionally controls receptivity (Zhou et al. 2014). pC1 is heterogeneous, however: later work assigns receptivity and mating status mainly to pC1a and related subtypes, and aggression/persistent state to pC1d/pC1e.
source_title: Central brain neurons expressing doublesex regulate female receptivity in Drosophila
authors: Zhou C, Pan Y, Robinett CC, Meissner GW, Baker BS

claim: The post-mating switch requires SPR in a small set of fru+/ppk+ (also dsx+) sensory neurons of the female reproductive tract, later called SPSNs. Silencing these neurons in virgins mimics the mated state (lower receptivity, more egg laying). This led to the model that sex peptide acts by reducing their activity; the 2008-2009 papers inferred this silencing rather than recording it directly.
source_title: A receptor that mediates the post-mating switch in Drosophila reproductive behaviour; Sensory neurons in the Drosophila genital tract regulate female reproductive behavior
authors: Yapici N, Kim YJ, Ribeiro C, Dickson BJ (2008); Hasemeyer M, Yapici N, Heberlein U, Dickson BJ (2009); also Yang CH et al. (2009) Neuron

claim: SAG ascending neurons in the abdominal ganglion receive SPSN input and carry mating-status information to the central brain. Silencing SAG makes virgin females less receptive and raises egg laying, mimicking the mated state. The downstream SAG-to-pC1 connection was established later by EM connectomics (Wang F et al. 2020).
source_title: Ascending SAG neurons control sexual receptivity of Drosophila females
authors: Feng K, Palfreyman MT, Hasemeyer M, Talsma A, Dickson BJ

claim: oviDNs are command-like descending neurons for egg laying. They receive excitatory (oviEN) and inhibitory (oviIN) inputs, and pC1 neurons, which carry mating-status input from SAG, feed into this circuit. This is the egg-laying circuit, not the ovipositor-extrusion rejection circuit. Evidence: causal manipulations plus EM connectivity (FAFB and/or hemibrain; dataset to be confirmed).
source_title: Neural circuitry linking mating and egg laying in Drosophila females
authors: Wang F, Wang K, Forknall N, Patrick C, Yang T, Parekh R, Bock D, Dickson BJ

claim: DNp13 descending neurons are command-type neurons for ovipositor extrusion (OE), and OE deters males only when mated females perform it. DNp13 respond to male song through direct synaptic input from pC2l auditory neurons. Mating status does not change DNp13 song responses; it changes how well DNp13 engage the OE motor circuits. That status signal comes from ppk+ uterine sensory neurons that are activated at ovulation. Vaginal plate opening and OE are controlled by anatomically and functionally distinct circuits.
source_title: Circuit and behavioral mechanisms of sexual rejection by Drosophila females
authors: Wang F, Wang K, Forknall N, Parekh R, Dickson BJ

claim: Vaginal plate opening (VPO), the virgin female's acceptance signal, is controlled by a pair of female-specific descending neurons (vpoDNs). vpoDNs receive excitatory input from auditory vpoEN neurons tuned to specific features of D. melanogaster courtship song, and from pC1 neurons that encode the female's mating status.
source_title: Neural circuit mechanisms of sexual receptivity in Drosophila females
authors: Wang K, Wang F, Forknall N, Yang T, Patrick C, Parekh R, Dickson BJ

species: Drosophila melanogaster, virgin females and males
claim: In virgin females, ovipositor extrusion signals ACCEPTANCE. It prompts males to attempt copulation and helps the transition from courtship to copulation, unlike the rejection role of extrusion in mated females.
source_title: Ovipositor extrusion promotes the transition from courtship to copulation and signals female acceptance in Drosophila melanogaster
authors: Mezzera C, Brotas M, Gaspar M, ... Vasconcelos ML

claim: In females, optogenetic activation of pC1d/pC1e neurons triggers a persistent internal state lasting minutes that raises female aggression. Imaging showed long-lasting activity. EM reconstruction in the FAFB volume via FlyWire (the hemibrain may have been used for comparison) revealed recurrent connectivity among pC1d, pC1e and aIPg that could hold that state.
source_title: The neural basis for a persistent internal state in Drosophila females
authors: Deutsch D, Pacheco D, Encarnacion-Rivera L, Pereira T, Fathy R, Clemens J, Girardin C, Calhoun A, Ireland E, Burke A, Dorkenwald S, McKellar C, Macrina T, Lu R, Lee K, Kemnitz N, Ih D, Castro M, Halageri A, Jordan C, Silversmith W, Wu J, Seung HS, Murthy M

claim: aIPg neurons, downstream of pC1d, drive female aggression (head-butting, shoving). Split-GAL4 lines plus hemibrain connectivity defined the cell types in the female aggression circuit.
source_title: Cell types and neuronal circuitry underlying female aggression in Drosophila
authors: Schretter CE, Aso Y, Robie AA, Dreher M, Dolan MJ, Chen N, Ito M, Yang T, Parekh R, Branson KM, Rubin GM

claim: Activating P1 neurons in males produces a persistent internal state that raises male-male aggression, lasting minutes after stimulation ends. So P1 is an arousal/state hub, not just a courtship 'command' neuron.
source_title: P1 interneurons promote a persistent internal state that enhances inter-male aggression
authors: Hoopfer ED, Jung Y, Inagaki HK, Rubin GM, Anderson DJ (see also Jung Y et al. 2020 Neuron on P1a)

claim: Males pattern their song in real time using feedback cues from the female. The choice between pulse and sine song depends on male-female distance and female speed (Coen et al. 2014). Song amplitude is adjusted to distance (Coen et al. 2016). Visual cues contribute, but vision was not shown to be the sole or main channel.
source_title: Dynamic sensory cues shape song structure in Drosophila
authors: Coen P, Clemens J, Weinstein AJ, Pacheco DA, Deng Y, Murthy M

claim: In females, ppk25-expressing pheromone-sensing neurons promote receptivity to male courtship. The same channel subunit also supports male courtship, so contact chemosensation matters on the female side too.
source_title: Drosophila pheromone-sensing neurons expressing the ppk25 ion channel subunit stimulate male courtship and female receptivity
authors: Vijayan V, Thistle R, Liu T, Starostina E, Pikielny CW

claim: FlyWire (a single adult female brain, about 139k neurons, hemibrain-matched cell types) lets researchers trace brain-level social inputs, including LC visual neurons, DA1 pheromone PNs and the brain axons of ascending neurons, to the female pC1 cluster and descending neurons. It is wiring only. It lacks the nerve cord and leg sensory neurons, so full contact-pheromone paths need BANC or male-CNS data, and male-specific circuits such as P1 are absent.
source_title: Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain; Whole-brain annotation and multi-connectome cell typing of Drosophila
authors: Dorkenwald S et al.; Schlegel P et al. (FlyWire Consortium)

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male (single CNS) vs female
claim: The complete male CNS connectome (brain plus nerve cord, one animal; about 166,700 neurons and 11,710 neuron types, fully proofread and annotated for fruitless/doublesex expression) was compared with the female FlyWire brain at synaptic resolution. It found 8,069 isomorphic, 138 dimorphic, 289 male-specific and 71 female-specific types. Sex-specific or dimorphic neurons make up 4.8% of male and 2.4% of female central-brain neurons. They cluster in higher-order centres while the sensory and motor periphery is largely isomorphic, and dimorphism spreads through dimorphic connectivity. Dimorphism status matches fru/dsx expression closely but not perfectly.
source_title: Sexual dimorphism in the complete connectome of the Drosophila male central nervous system
authors: Berg S, Beckett IR, Costa M, Schlegel P, ... Jefferis GSXE and collaborators (Janelia FlyEM / Cambridge)
venue: bioRxiv preprint 2025; Cell (Sept 2026, per program context)

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male, freely moving (head cuticle window, retroreflective-marker tracking)
claim: In freely walking, socially interacting male D. melanogaster, ratiometric imaging through a head window (Flyception2) showed fruitless-expressing P1 neurons active during courtship but inactive during copulation, while GABAergic mAL neurons stayed active during copulation.
source_title: Imaging brain activity during complex social behaviors in Drosophila with Flyception2
authors: Grover D, Katsuki T, Li J, Dawkins TJ, Greenspan RJ

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male, head-fixed on air-supported ball
claim: In tethered males courting a moving dot in virtual reality, P1 activity tracks moment-to-moment pursuit intensity, and the gain of LC10a visual projection neurons is selectively raised during courtship.
source_title: Sexual arousal gates visual processing during Drosophila courtship
authors: Hindmarsh Sten T, Li R, Otopalik A, Ruta V

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male, two-photon imaging during song (exact prep/elicitation not confirmed in snippets)
claim: Calcium imaging of the ventral nerve cord during singing showed nested song-motor populations: dPR1 neurons are selectively active during pulse song, while TN1A neurons are active during both pulse and sine song.
source_title: Activity of nested neural circuits drives different courtship songs in Drosophila
authors: Shiozaki HM, Wang K, Lillvis JL, Xu M, Dickson BJ, Stern DL

claim: Brain recordings showed the same nested activation in the two descending pathways needed for song (pIP10 and pMP2), and connectome analysis showed these pathways give structured input to VNC song neurons consistent with that pattern.
source_title: Activity of nested neural circuits drives different courtship songs in Drosophila
authors: Shiozaki HM et al.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the descending neuron pIP10 induces both pulse and sine song, whereas pMP2 activation induces pulse but not sine song.
source_title: Activity of nested neural circuits drives different courtship songs in Drosophila
authors: Shiozaki HM et al.

claim: Lillvis et al. (2024, Curr Biol 34:808-824) built split-GAL4 lines for VNC song-circuit cell types and scored song automatically (reported as SongExplorer, which separates pulse from sine). With activation and silencing they showed that pulse and sine song come from nested neural circuits. The exact counts (58 lines, at least 40 cell types) still need checking against the paper.
source_title: Nested neural circuits generate distinct acoustic signals during Drosophila courtship
authors: Lillvis JL, Wang K, Shiozaki HM, Xu M, Stern DL, Dickson BJ

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male (imaging under optogenetic drive, not natural singing)
claim: Two-photon imaging of TN1 wing-motor neurons during optogenetic pIP10 drive: nearly half were positively correlated with the stimulus, while a smaller fraction were anti-correlated, with alternating peaks that persisted after stimulation. Behaviorally, males sang simple one-mode trains far from the female and alternating sequences near her.
source_title: Flexible circuit mechanisms for context-dependent song sequencing
authors: Roemschied FA, Pacheco DA, Aragon MJ, Ireland EC, Li X, Thieringer K, Pang R, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult males and females, head-fixed
claim: Whole-central-brain volumetric imaging with cross-brain registration found auditory activity in most central-brain regions, with most of it tuned to courtship-song features. Responses were stereotyped in early mechanosensory regions and more variable in higher regions, and this variability was largely independent of ongoing movement.
source_title: Auditory activity is diverse and widespread throughout the central brain of Drosophila
authors: Pacheco DA, Thiberge SY, Pnevmatikakis E, Murthy M

claim: Light beads microscopy recorded brain-wide calcium signals in behaving adult flies at 28 volumes/s (60 volumes/s for the central brain alone). It revealed fast auditory responses that standard volumetric two-photon imaging misses, and temporal super-resolution recovered responses to single courtship-song pulses.
source_title: High-speed whole-brain imaging in Drosophila
authors: Gauthey et al.

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult males and females
claim: Dsx+ pC2 neurons (pC2l and pC2m) are tuned to several temporal features of pulse song, with similar tuning in males and females. This comes from two-photon imaging of pC2 cell bodies and of Dsx+ neurites in the lateral junction (LJ), a neuropil region, not a cell type. Optogenetic pC2 activation drives sex-specific behaviours, including song production in males.
source_title: Shared Song Detector Neurons in Drosophila Male and Female Brains Drive Sex-Specific Behaviors
authors: Deutsch D, Clemens J, Thiberge SY, Guan G, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult virgin female, head-fixed
claim: In virgin females, the female-specific descending neurons vpoDN showed strong calcium rises in soma and neurites during playback of male courtship song (GCaMP6s, two-photon). They receive excitatory input from song-tuned vpoEN auditory neurons and from pC1.
source_title: Neural circuit mechanisms of sexual receptivity in Drosophila females
authors: Wang F, Wang K, Forknall N, Patrick C, Yang T, Parekh R, Bock D, Dickson BJ
venue: Nature (seed-style attribution to Neuron is incorrect)

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult female (virgin vs mated)
claim: After mating, song responses of vpoDNs, but not of the upstream auditory vpoENs, are attenuated, which can explain why mated females are less receptive. pC1 neurons, which encode mating status and excite vpoDNs, are implicated as the source of this modulation.
source_title: Neural circuit mechanisms of sexual receptivity in Drosophila females
authors: Wang F et al.

claim: In females, optogenetic activation of Dsx+ pC1 neurons (notably pC1d/e) produces a persistent internal state lasting minutes that changes receptivity, responses to song and aggression-like behaviour. pC1 and Fru+ aIPg neurons show persistent activity after pC1 activation, and EM wiring (FAFB/FlyWire, female) shows strong recurrent pC1d/e-aIPg connections. Later work separates the contributions of pC1d and pC1e.
source_title: The neural basis for a persistent internal state in Drosophila females
authors: Deutsch D, Pacheco D, Encarnacion-Rivera L, Pereira T, Fathy R, Clemens J, Girardin C, Calhoun A, Ireland E, Burke A, Dorkenwald S, McKellar C, Macrina T, Lu R, Lee K, Kemnitz N, Ih D, Castro M, Halageri A, Jordan C, Silversmith W, Wu J, Seung HS, Murthy M (author list from memory; only 'Deutsch et al.' confirmed in results)

claim: Baker et al. (2022) imaged and characterised 24 new auditory cell types in the fly brain (activity-recorded). Using the FlyWire female-brain connectome, they mapped connections among these types and to known early and higher-order auditory neurons (connectome-wiring). Neurons with different song-mode preferences are highly interconnected in a network without clear hierarchy, but each cell type's responses can be predicted from its inputs.
source_title: Neural network organization for courtship-song feature detection in Drosophila
authors: Baker CA, McKellar C, Pang R, Nern A, Dorkenwald S, Pacheco DA, Eckstein N, Funke J, Dickson BJ, Murthy M (list from memory; Baker, Clemens?, Murthy confirmed only generally)

claim: HI-FISH (HCR-3.0 in situ hybridization for the immediate-early gene Hr38) maps activated cells across the whole adult male brain. Double labeling showed activity of aggression-promoting classes, including male-specific P1a, during courtship and aggression, and opto-HI-FISH identified candidate downstream targets.
source_title: Whole-brain in situ mapping of neuronal activation in Drosophila during social behaviors and optogenetic stimulation
authors: Anderson lab, Caltech (first author not confirmed in search snippets)

claim: CaMPARI photoconverts green to red when high calcium coincides with about 405 nm light. It has been used to mark active neurons in several intact, freely moving adult flies at once during a stimulus-defined window. Its use for social or group behaviours such as courtship is proposed rather than shown in that study.
source_title: The Photoconvertible Fluorescent Probe, CaMPARI, Labels Active Neurons in Freely-Moving Intact Adult Fruit Flies
authors: (Frontiers in Neural Circuits authors not confirmed in snippets)

claim: TRIC, a transcriptional reporter of intracellular calcium, monitors slow changes in activity. Examples include neuropeptide F neurons responding to sexual deprivation, and pars intercerebralis cells responding to food and arousal.
source_title: A transcriptional reporter of intracellular Ca2+ in Drosophila
authors: Gao XJ, Riabinina O, Li J, Potter CJ, Clandinin TR, Luo L

claim: Light-field microscopy imaged the near-whole adult fly brain at up to 200 Hz with pan-neuronal GCaMP6 and found a global increase in activity when the fly walks compared with when it rests.
source_title: Fast near-whole-brain imaging in adult Drosophila during responses to stimuli and behavior
authors: Aimon S, Katsuki T, Jia T, Grosenick L, Broxton M, Deisseroth K, Sejnowski TJ, Greenspan RJ

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult, head-fixed, spontaneous behavior
claim: SCAPE imaging of a large volume of the adult fly brain, in head-fixed flies behaving spontaneously, showed that most neurons' activity correlated or anti-correlated with running and flailing over timescales from seconds to about a minute. Grooming elicited a weaker global response. Residual activity was high-dimensional and organized in small, spatially clustered groups of neurons.
source_title: The spatial and temporal structure of neural activity across the fly brain
authors: Schaffer ES et al. (Hillman, Axel, Abbott labs)

claim: Volumetric two-photon imaging of pan-neuronal GCaMP across the central brain of head-fixed walking flies, registered to a common atlas, found spatially clustered supervoxel-level signals selective for forward or angular velocity. The signals are not resolved to identified neurons.
source_title: Mapping the neural dynamics of locomotion across the Drosophila brain
authors: Brezovec BE, Berger AB, Hao YA, Chen F, Druckmann S, Clandinin TR

claim: BIFROST registers in vivo multiphoton brains to a Functional Drosophila Atlas (FDA) with under 10 µm precision across specimens and labs, and aligns the hemibrain and FlyWire connectomes to the FDA.
source_title: BIFROST: A method for registering diverse imaging datasets of the Drosophila brain
authors: Brezovec BE, Berger AB, Hao YA, Lin A, Ahmed OM, Pacheco DA, Thiberge SY, Murthy M, Clandinin TR

claim: If the claim stays attributed to Mann, Gallen & Clandinin 2017, narrow it to: 'Resting-state functional connectivity from whole-brain calcium imaging was strongly associated with the strength of both direct and indirect anatomical pathways, and some regions showed considerably higher functional connectivity than their direct anatomical connections predict.' The claim as worded (strong relation to direct region-to-region structural connectivity; mushroom body more dependent on indirect connections) is the finding of Turner, Mann & Clandinin 2021.
source_title: Whole-brain calcium imaging reveals an intrinsic functional network in Drosophila
authors: Mann K, Gallen CL, Clandinin TR

claim: Applying fMRI methods to fly whole-brain calcium imaging together with FlyEM and FlyWire connectomes, the correlation between functional and structural connectivity fell linearly as the number of regions increased (the same trend as in humans). Neurons with unsegregated pre- and postsynaptic sites showed higher correlation between the two.
source_title: Functional connectivity, structural connectivity, and inter-individual variability in Drosophila melanogaster
authors: Okuno T et al.

claim: NeuronBridge is a web application that matches light-microscopy images of GAL4 and split-GAL4 lines (FlyLight) to EM-reconstructed neurons (FlyEM connectomes) by morphology.
source_title: NeuronBridge: an intuitive web application for neuronal morphology search across large data sets
authors: Clements J et al.

claim: A split-GAL4 resource provides 3,060 lines targeting cell types in the adult Drosophila CNS and 1,373 lines for third-instar larvae, related to EM connectomes through NeuronBridge and other search tools.
source_title: A split-GAL4 driver line resource for Drosophila neuron types
authors: Meissner GW et al. (FlyLight Project Team)

claim: FlyWire annotation identified 8,453 cell types in the adult female brain: 3,643 previously proposed in the hemibrain and 4,581 new, mostly outside the hemibrain volume.
source_title: Whole-brain annotation and multi-connectome cell typing of Drosophila
authors: Schlegel P et al.

claim: In C. elegans, the NeuroPAL multicolor transgene gives every neuron a stereotyped color map that resolves all neuronal identities while leaving green channels free for GCaMP. This enabled brain-wide, identity-resolved activity recordings in response to chemosensory cues.
source_title: NeuroPAL: A Multicolor Atlas for Whole-Brain Neuronal Identification in C. elegans
authors: Yemini E, Lin A, Nejatbakhsh A, Varol E, Sun R, Mena GE, Samuel ADT, Paninski L, Venkatachalam V, Hobert O

claim: Optogenetic activation plus whole-brain calcium imaging of 23,433 neuron pairs in the C. elegans head showed that measured signal propagation differs from anatomy-based predictions. Mutant experiments showed extrasynaptic signaling contributes to the difference.
source_title: Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans
authors: Randi F, Sharma AK, Dvali S, Leifer AM

claim: In larval zebrafish, a functionally imaged EM (CLEM) dataset of the anterior hindbrain identified morphological cell types whose activity patterns define distinct computational roles in visual evidence accumulation, with bilateral inhibition, disinhibition and recurrent connectivity as key motifs. A separate photoconversion-based pipeline labeled and reconstructed functionally characterized neurons across other animals and trained a classifier that predicts functional identity from morphology alone.
source_title: Correlative light and electron microscopy reveals the fine circuit structure underlying evidence accumulation in larval zebrafish
authors: (author list not verified in search results)

claim: In D. melanogaster females, Johnston's organ auditory sensory neurons express three dopamine receptor types, and some receive direct synapses from dopaminergic neurons. Knocking down Dop1R2 reduces their sound responses in unmated but not mated females, and Dop1R2 in these neurons enhances unmated females' song-evoked copulation receptivity. This implicates Dop1R2-mediated dopaminergic modulation in mating-state-dependent auditory processing (iScience 2025).
source_title: Mating status-dependent dopaminergic modulation of auditory sensory neurons in Drosophila
authors: (not seen)

claim: A Rockefeller University news story on the Ruta lab's virtual-courtship rig reports that P1 neurons 'light up' as a tethered male begins running and wing-flapping toward a dot that mimics female motion.
source_title: Identifying the spark of desire in fruit flies
authors: Rockefeller University news office

claim: A leaky integrate-and-fire model of the entire adult Drosophila central brain, built only from FlyWire synaptic connectivity and predicted neurotransmitter identity, predicts neurons that respond to tastes and are required for feeding initiation when sugar- or water-sensing gustatory neurons are activated in silico.
source_title: A Drosophila computational brain model reveals sensorimotor processing
authors: Shiu PK et al.

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult female brain connectome; validation in behaving/imaged flies
claim: In the Shiu whole-brain model, activating Johnston's organ mechanosensory neurons predicts a small antennal-grooming circuit (aBN1, aBN2, aDN1, aDN2). It also makes a non-obvious prediction: JO-CE neurons drive robust aBN1 activity but JO-F neurons do not, despite synapsing directly onto aBN1. This was tested by optogenetic activation of each JON population plus calcium imaging in aBN1.
source_title: A Drosophila computational brain model reveals sensorimotor processing
authors: Shiu PK et al.

claim: A connectome-constrained network of 64 optic-lobe motion-pathway cell types, with unknown single-neuron and synapse parameters optimized by deep learning for motion detection, made single-neuron activity predictions that agreed with experimental measurements across 26 studies. These included ON/OFF channel separation and T4/T5 direction selectivity.
source_title: Connectome-constrained networks predict neural activity across the fly visual system
authors: Lappalainen JK, ... Macke JH, Turaga SC

claim: Theory and simulations show that connectome data alone are generally insufficient to predict neural activity when biophysical parameters are uncertain. Pairing connectivity with recordings from a subset of neurons can accurately predict activity in unrecorded neurons.
source_title: Prediction of neural activity in connectome-constrained recurrent networks
authors: Beiran M, Litwin-Kumar A

claim: flybody is a whole-body, anatomically detailed physics model of Drosophila melanogaster in MuJoCo, with new models for fluid and adhesion forces. It reproduced realistic walking and flight using reinforcement learning, not connectome-driven control.
source_title: Whole-body physics simulation of fruit fly locomotion
authors: Vaxenburg R, Siwanowicz I, Merel J, et al.

claim: NeuroMechFly v2 adds vision, olfaction, ascending motor feedback and complex terrain to a neuromechanical adult fly. It demonstrated fly-fly following using a connectome-constrained visual network.
source_title: NeuroMechFly v2: simulating embodied sensorimotor control in adult Drosophila
authors: Wang-Chen S, Stimpfling VA, Lam TKC, Özdil PG, Genoud L, Hurtak F, Ramdya P

species: Drosophila melanogaster (FlyWire female brain model + simulated body)
claim: Eon Systems (a company, March 2026 demo) coupled the Shiu et al. whole-brain model to the NeuroMechFly v2 body in a closed loop. It read out a small, hand-picked set of descending neurons and translated them into high-level commands (turn, walk forward, groom, feed) executed by pre-trained motor controllers.
source_title: How the Eon Team Produced a Virtual Embodied Fly
authors: Eon Systems

claim: One 2026 blog post ('No, we haven't uploaded a fly yet', Substack/LessWrong; not peer-reviewed) criticised the Eon 'uploaded fly' framing. It noted that the descending interface reads out only a few of the fly's roughly 1,300 descending neurons, that brain-to-body mappings were chosen by hand, and that the LIF brain has no dendritic detail or plasticity. These limits are consistent with the published description of the Shiu et al. model.
source_title: No, we haven't uploaded a fly yet
authors: Preserving Hope (Substack; cross-posted to LessWrong)

claim: The State of Brain Emulation Report 2025 reassesses progress since the 2008 Sandberg and Bostrom roadmap. It is organized around recording neural dynamics, mapping connectomes, and emulation plus embodiment, and it identifies remaining challenges and strategic priorities.
source_title: State of Brain Emulation Report 2025
authors: Zanichelli N, Schons M, Freeman I, Shiu P, Arkhipov A

species: Drosophila melanogaster, MANC (male VNC) and other VNC connectomes; optogenetic validation in behaving flies
claim: Dynamic simulations of fly ventral nerve cord connectomes identified DNg100 as the top descending driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. They isolated a minimal three-interneuron rhythm generator (one inhibitory, two excitatory) that was necessary and sufficient in simulation across four connectome datasets. They also predicted that DNb08 drives rhythmic leg movement, which optogenetics confirmed in behaving flies.
source_title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator circuit for fly walking
authors: Pugliese SM et al. (with Shiu PK and colleagues)

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult male VNC (MANC) plus behavioral manipulation
claim: By activating and silencing more than 40 cell types in behaving males while recording song, plus wiring from the male VNC connectome (MANC), Lillvis et al. identified a core nerve-cord song circuit. It has eight fru- and/or dsx-expressing cell types in two nested feedforward pathways: the smaller drives sine song, and the larger, which includes the smaller, drives pulse song. Evidence type: causal-manipulation plus connectome-wiring.
source_title: Nested neural circuits generate distinct acoustic signals during Drosophila courtship
authors: Lillvis JL et al.

claim: A compact circuit model shows that a few computations suffice to replicate context-dependent song. Weak sensory input to a direct brain-to-VNC excitatory pathway yields simple one-mode song far from the female. Strong input plus P1a-mediated disinhibition of the VNC song premotor circuit yields complex alternating sequences near her.
source_title: Flexible circuit mechanisms for context-dependent song sequencing
authors: Roemschied FA et al. (Murthy lab)

claim: The same male brain neurons that drive air-borne courtship song also control substrate-borne vibration through separate premotor pathways. The shared circuit uses recurrence and mutual inhibition, and coordinates the signals with locomotion so vibrations occur only when they can reach the female. A circuit model is released as code.
source_title: A neural circuit for context-dependent multimodal signaling in Drosophila
authors: Steinfath E, Khalili A, Stenger M, Schultze BL, Ravindran Nair S, Alizadeh K, Clemens J

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult brain (imaging) + FlyWire female connectome
claim: Baker et al. identified 24 new intermediate auditory cell types and mapped all their synaptic connections in FlyWire. They measured each cell's pulse vs sine preference, sine-frequency tuning and pulse-rate tuning, finding a continuum of song-mode preferences. The results support interconnectivity, rather than separate pulse and sine pathways, as the source of that continuum.
source_title: Neural network organization for courtship-song feature detection in Drosophila
authors: Baker CA, McKellar C, Pang R, ... Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult males and females (pC2l); females (vpo neurons)
claim: Calcium imaging shows pC2l neurons in males and females respond selectively to pulse-song features, from single-pulse frequency to pulse-train length, and weakly to sine (Deutsch et al. 2019). In females, vpoDN and its song-responsive inputs vpoEN are tuned to features of D. melanogaster courtship song (Wang et al. 2021; pulse-specific tuning unconfirmed, see Track 03). These are activity-recorded results from separate studies, summarised in Baker et al. 2022.
source_title: Neural Network Organization for Courtship Song Feature Detection in Drosophila (bioRxiv v2, citing prior recordings)
authors: Baker CA et al. (summarizing Deutsch et al. 2019 and others)

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult males during courtship; silencing of 23 LC types
claim: A deep network trained with 'knockout training', in which silencing of individual visual projection neuron types in behaving males is mirrored by removing matching model units, gives a one-to-one mapping between model units and LC neuron types. It shows that combinations of visual projection neurons form a population code driving male courtship interactions with the female.
source_title: Mapping model units to visual neurons reveals population code for social behaviour
authors: Cowley BR, Calhoun AJ, Rangarajan N, Ireland E, Turner MH, Pillow JW, Murthy M

claim: During courtship, males pattern their song using feedback cues from the female. An unsupervised model (GLM-HMM) uncovers three hidden states, each with a different mapping from feedback cues to song mode, and predicts moment-to-moment song-patterning decisions. A neuron pair previously considered song command neurons is sufficient to drive switching between states.
source_title: Unsupervised identification of the internal states that shape natural behavior
authors: Calhoun AJ, Pillow JW, Murthy M

claim: The complete connectome of the Drosophila male central nervous system contains 166,700 neurons across brain and nerve cord, joined through an intact neck, with fruitless/doublesex annotation and 11,710 neuron types. Compared with female data it finds 8,069 isomorphic, 138 dimorphic, 289 male-specific and 71 female-specific types.
source_title: Sexual dimorphism in the complete Drosophila male central nervous system connectome
authors: Berg S et al. (Janelia FlyEM, Cambridge Connectomics, Google Research)

claim: BANC is a synapse-resolution connectome of the brain and nerve cord of one adult female fly (take exact neuron and synapse counts from the paper). Its wiring shows effector neurons mainly influenced by sensory neurons in the same body part, forming local feedback loops. These loops are linked by long-range ascending and descending neurons organised into behaviour-centred modules. Evidence type: connectome-wiring only.
source_title: Distributed control circuits across a brain-and-cord connectome
authors: Bates AS et al. (BANC consortium, Wilson lab and others)

claim: A neural network predicting six transmitters (acetylcholine, glutamate, GABA, serotonin, dopamine, octopamine) from EM images is 87% accurate per synapse, 94% per neuron and 91% for known cell types.
source_title: Neurotransmitter classification from electron microscopy images at synaptic sites in Drosophila melanogaster
authors: Eckstein N et al.

species: Drosophila melanogaster, two adult female brains (FlyWire, hemibrain)
claim: Joint analysis of the FlyWire and hemibrain connectomes found broad stereotypy but occasional differences in neuron counts and connectivity between individuals. About one-third of cell types proposed for the hemibrain could not be reliably re-identified in FlyWire.
source_title: Whole-brain annotation and multi-connectome cell typing of Drosophila
authors: Schlegel P et al.

species: Drosophila melanogaster, head-fixed adults (imaging) + FlyWire connectome
claim: A whole-brain model constrained by the FlyWire connectome, fit to calcium recordings of spontaneous activity in head-fixed flies, reproduced three features it was not trained on: lognormal synaptic weights, scale-free neuronal avalanches, and short intrinsic time constants in visual cells. In silico perturbations suggested a sparse, brain-spanning ensemble of inhibitory hub neurons is necessary and sufficient to sustain resting dynamics.
source_title: Connectome-constrained modeling identifies neurons and synapses that sustain spontaneous activity in Drosophila
authors: (bioRxiv preprint; authors not captured in search results)

claim: A related method fits a firing-rate model constrained by the FlyWire connectome to whole-brain calcium imaging online. It treats synaptic weights, neuronal time constants and background input strengths as unknowns to be fitted, with the connectome fixing only the network topology.
source_title: Online Fitting of a Connectome-Constrained Drosophila Whole-Brain Model to Calcium Imaging Data
authors: (OpenReview submission; authors not captured)

species: Drosophila melanogaster connectome used as network architecture
claim: FlyGM (arXiv 2602.17997, 2026; peer-review and venue status unconfirmed) uses the fly whole-brain connectome as a signed, directed message-passing graph to control simulated whole-body walking, turning and flight. In imitation learning it trained faster and reached lower loss than random-graph, rewired-graph and MLP baselines. This shows the connectome helps as a network design choice for a trained controller, not biological fidelity.
source_title: Whole-Brain Connectomic Graph Model Enables Whole-Body Locomotion Control in Fruit Fly
authors: Tsinghua University group

claim: LLantia (Yin and Cardona, arXiv 2026, unreviewed) uses an LLM to extract cell-type function descriptions from the literature, then combines them with the connectome to propose functions for other Drosophila brain cell types. The extent of validation is unconfirmed, and its outputs should be treated as hypotheses for experimental testing.
source_title: Neural Circuit Function Inference with LLMs
authors: Yin Y, Cardona A

species: Drosophila melanogaster (whole-brain calcium imaging vs FlyEM/FlyWire)
claim: Okuno et al. (2025, eLife reviewed preprint) applied fMRI-style methods to fly whole-brain calcium imaging with the FlyEM/FlyWire connectomes. The correlation between functional and structural connectivity fell linearly as the number of regions rose, and neurons with unsegregated synapses (by a new pre/post-synaptic segregation index) showed higher functional-structural correlation.
source_title: Functional connectivity, structural connectivity, and inter-individual variability in Drosophila melanogaster
authors: (eLife reviewed preprint; authors not captured)

claim: Shiozaki et al. (2024, Nature Neuroscience; Stern lab with Dickson-lab collaborators) imaged calcium activity of nerve-cord song-circuit neurons in singing males. Activity is nested: neurons active during sine song are also active during pulse song, and pulse song recruits additional neurons. This is consistent with the nested pathways identified by Lillvis et al. 2024.
source_title: Activity of nested neural circuits drives different courtship songs in Drosophila
authors: Shiozaki HM et al. (from memory; not confirmed in results)
