species: Drosophila melanogaster male CNS connectome (MaleCNS v1.0)
claim: flymsg is an unreviewed 2026 GitHub project (releases v0.5.0/v0.5.1) that runs a whole-CNS leaky integrate-and-fire model on the MaleCNS v1.0 connectome, following Shiu et al. (Nature 2024). Its stated departures from Shiu's model are a synaptic weight rescaled for MaleCNS's denser synapse detection (w_syn 0.275/1.43 = 0.192) and no adaptive threshold (kept as an option). Its 'validation' is 29 self-defined pass/fail checks (29/29 under its own 'criterion v4') plus agreement with Shiu's brian2 model on the same connectome. The checks test whether the simulation reproduces qualitatively known circuit functions (LC4 to Giant Fiber looming escape, P1 to pIP10 song pathway, sugar to MN9, bitter leaving MN9 silent), with controls, dose-response and latency-order tests. They are not quantitative comparisons with recorded neural activity. Any new outputs it reports are untested model predictions.
source_title: flymsg: Simulate and view in 3D the complete male Drosophila CNS connectome
authors: gianlucamazza (GitHub)

species: Drosophila melanogaster; freely behaving wild-type male courting a virgin female in a multi-microphone chamber
claim: Male D. melanogaster pattern courtship song moment to moment using feedback from the female. Whether a male sings pulse or sine song, and how bouts are structured, is largely predicted by female movement cues (her speed, and the male-female distance and position). Much song variability that looked stochastic is therefore driven by female feedback, and it depends on the male's sensory (largely visual) access to her.
source_title: Dynamic sensory cues shape song structure in Drosophila
authors: Coen P, Clemens J, Weinstein AJ, Pacheco DA, Deng Y, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster; freely courting male with virgin female
claim: Male flies scale song amplitude with distance to the female, singing louder when farther away. This roughly compensates for the steep distance-dependent fall-off of near-field courtship sound, so the male adjusts signal intensity to the receiver's position.
source_title: Sensorimotor transformations underlying variability in song intensity during Drosophila courtship
authors: Coen P, Xie M, Clemens J, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster; freely courting males; optogenetic activation of P1/pC1 in males
claim: A GLM-HMM fit to natural male courtship identified three latent states. Each state has a different mapping from female feedback cues to song mode, and together they predict moment-to-moment song choices. Activating a neuron pair previously described as song command neurons (likely pIP10; confirm in the full text) was sufficient to drive switching between states.
source_title: Unsupervised identification of the internal states that shape natural behavior
authors: Calhoun AJ, Pillow JW, Murthy M

claim: Two pulse-song types, Pfast and Pslow, were discovered in male D. melanogaster. Males choose between them according to their distance to and position relative to the female (Pslow tends to be used when close), which adds another feedback-dependent channel to the song.
source_title: Discovery of a new song mode in Drosophila reveals hidden structure in the sensory and neural drivers of behavior
authors: Clemens J, Coen P, Roemschied FA, Pereira TD, Mazumder D, Aldarondo DE, Pacheco DA, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster; males, courting versus solitary with optogenetic activation
claim: Male D. melanogaster sing simple single-mode trains far from the female and complex pulse-sine sequences near her. Roemschied et al. (2023) combined optogenetic manipulation (e.g., P1a, pIP10) with circuit modeling. They propose that a single brain-to-VNC pathway operates in two regimes set by recent sensory history, not parallel circuits. Brief input drives simple song. Prolonged input recruits disinhibition of VNC song circuits, which are built on mutual inhibition and rebound excitability, and so enables complex sequences near the female.
source_title: Flexible circuit mechanisms for context-dependent song sequencing
authors: Roemschied FA, Pacheco DA, Aragon MJ, Ireland EC, Li X, Thieringer K, Pang R, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster; males (courtship behavior with LC silencing); imaging of LC neurons
claim: Silencing individual types of lobula columnar (LC) visual projection neuron, combined with 'knockout training' of a deep network and calcium imaging, showed that the male's representation of the female that drives courtship behaviors, including song, is distributed across a population of LC types. It is not carried by a single dedicated channel.
source_title: Mapping model units to visual neurons reveals population code for social behaviour
authors: Cowley BR, Calhoun AJ, Rangarajan N, Ireland E, Turner MH, Pillow JW, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster; tethered males in visual VR; two-photon imaging and optogenetic P1 activation
claim: In tethered D. melanogaster males walking on a ball, pursuit of a moving fly-sized visual target depends on P1-mediated sexual arousal. Two-photon imaging with optogenetic P1 activation showed that arousal gates how LC10a visual signals drive the pursuit. Whether the target was presented in closed or open loop, and the exact circuit site of the gating, need confirmation.
source_title: Sexual arousal gates visual processing during Drosophila courtship
authors: Hindmarsh Sten T, Li R, Otopalik A, Ruta V

species: Drosophila melanogaster; solitary males, intact and decapitated; dTRPA1 thermogenetic activation
claim: Thermogenetic activation of fruitless-expressing neurons elicits courtship song with no female present. The brain neurons P1 and the descending neuron pIP10 drive song in solitary males, and thoracic song neurons (e.g., dPR1, vPR6) shape song features even in decapitated flies. Song can therefore be 'written' neurally.
source_title: Neuronal control of Drosophila courtship song
authors: von Philipsborn AC, Liu T, Yu JY, Masser C, Bidaye SS, Dickson BJ

species: Drosophila melanogaster; virgin females; calcium imaging plus neuronal silencing and activation
claim: In virgin females, doublesex-expressing pC1 neurons respond to male courtship song and to the male pheromone cVA in calcium imaging. Silencing pC1 reduces receptivity, so pC1 acts as a multisensory receiver integrator.
source_title: Central brain neurons expressing doublesex regulate female receptivity in Drosophila
authors: Zhou C, Pan Y, Robinett CC, Meissner GW, Baker BS

species: Drosophila melanogaster; females and males; head-fixed two-photon imaging with song playback; optogenetic activation
claim: The doublesex-expressing neurons pC2l and pC2m exist in both sexes and respond selectively to conspecific pulse song, with inter-pulse-interval tuning that matches behavioral preferences. Activating them drives sex-specific behavioral responses to song.
source_title: Shared song detector neurons in Drosophila male and female brains drive sex-specific behaviors
authors: Deutsch D, Clemens J, Thiberge SY, Guan G, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster; virgin females; optogenetic activation, song playback, EM reconstruction
claim: Brief optogenetic activation of female pC1 neurons produces a persistent internal state lasting minutes that changes how females respond to male song playback, and it also elicits aggressive behaviors. EM reconstruction from FAFB showed recurrent connectivity among pC1 subtypes (notably pC1d/pC1e) consistent with the persistence.
source_title: The neural basis for a persistent internal state in Drosophila females
authors: Deutsch D, Pacheco D, Encarnacion-Rivera L, Pereira T, Fathy R, Clemens J, Girardin C, Calhoun A, Ireland E, Burke A, Dorkenwald S, McKellar C, Macrina T, Lu R, Lee K, Kemnitz N, Ih D, Castro M, Halageri A, Jordan C, Silversmith W, Wu J, Seung HS, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster; virgin and mated females; calcium imaging to song; optogenetic activation and silencing
claim: In D. melanogaster females, vpoDN descending neurons trigger vaginal plate opening, the acceptance behavior. vpoDN integrate excitatory input from vpoEN, which are tuned to features of D. melanogaster courtship song (pulse-specific tuning unconfirmed; see Track 03), with input from pC1 neurons that reflect mating status. Activating the pathway promotes VPO (Wang et al. 2021, Nature).
source_title: Neural circuit mechanisms of sexual receptivity in Drosophila females
authors: Wang K, Wang F, Forknall N, Yang T, Patrick C, Parekh R, Dickson BJ

species: Drosophila melanogaster; females paired with wingless males under song playback
claim: Playback of artificial pulse song with the conspecific inter-pulse interval (roughly mid-30 ms) sped up mating when females were paired with wingless (mute) males, whereas songs with other intervals were less effective. This showed that a playback signal can substitute for part of the male's side of the dialogue.
source_title: Pulse interval as a critical parameter in the courtship song of Drosophila melanogaster
authors: Bennet-Clark HC, Ewing AW

species: Drosophila melanogaster; male song recordings (various strains)
claim: The reported ~55 s oscillation in inter-pulse interval (Kyriacou-Hall song rhythm), and its claimed role in female preference, was not supported by large re-recordings and statistical reanalyses. The original authors dispute this and attribute the failures to pulse-detection problems and low-intensity courtship.
source_title: Experimental and statistical reevaluation provides no evidence for Drosophila courtship song rhythms (see also Stern 2014 BMC Biology; Kyriacou et al. 2017 PNAS rebuttal)
authors: Stern DL, Clemens J, Coen P, Calhoun AJ, Hogenesch JB, Arthur BJ, Murthy M

claim: D. melanogaster females produce their own wing-vibration song during copulation, and male seminal fluid modulates it. Acoustic signalling in fly courtship is therefore not one-way.
source_title: Female copulation song is modulated by seminal fluid
authors: Kerwin P, Yuan J, von Philipsborn AC

species: Drosophila melanogaster; freely walking and courting flies
claim: FlyMAD tracks freely walking flies and aims a laser at individual flies, even specific body regions, with low latency. It enabled thermogenetic or optogenetic activation of neurons such as P1 and pIP10 during ongoing courtship interactions.
source_title: FlyMAD: rapid thermogenetic control of neuronal activity in freely walking Drosophila
authors: Bath DE, Stowers JR, Hörmann D, Poehlmann A, Dickson BJ, Straw AD

species: Drosophila melanogaster song, plus bird and other animal vocalizations
claim: The Deep Audio Segmenter (DAS) annotates fly courtship song (pulse and sine) and bird song with deep networks, with latency low enough (milliseconds) for closed-loop experiments.
source_title: Fast and accurate annotation of acoustic signals with deep neural networks
authors: Steinfath E, Palacios-Muñoz A, Rottschäfer JR, Yuezak D, Clemens J

species: Drosophila melanogaster (courting pairs) and other species
claim: SLEAP multi-animal pose tracking can run inference in real time, fast enough for closed-loop control. The paper demonstrated closed-loop experiments in interacting flies.
source_title: SLEAP: A deep learning system for multi-animal pose tracking
authors: Pereira TD, Tabris N, Matsliah A, Turner DM, Li J, Ravindranath S, Papadoyannis ES, Normand E, Deutsch DS, Wang ZY, et al.

species: Periplaneta americana (American cockroach) groups with InsBot robots
claim: Autonomous robots coated with cockroach odor were accepted into groups of American cockroaches and shifted the mixed group's collective shelter choice, including toward a shelter the insects would not normally prefer. Robots and animals jointly determined the group decision.
source_title: Social integration of robots into groups of cockroaches to control self-organized choices
authors: Halloy J, Sempo G, Caprari G, Rivault C, Asadpour M, Tâche F, Saïd I, Durier V, Canonge S, Amé JM, Detrain C, Correll N, Martinoli A, Mondada F, Siegwart R, Deneubourg JL

species: Apis mellifera (juvenile honeybees) and Danio rerio (zebrafish), with robotic agents (ASSISIbf project)
claim: Robots placed in a honeybee arena (Graz, Austria) and a zebrafish tank (Lausanne, Switzerland) were linked, so each robot relayed its own group's behavior to the other. The two species' groups came to coordinate their collective decisions without ever meeting.
source_title: Robots mediating interactions between animals for interspecies collective behaviors
authors: Bonnet F, Mills R, Szopek M, Schönwetter-Fuchs S, Halloy J, Bogdan S, Correia L, Mondada F, Schmickl T

species: Apis mellifera; observation hive with a robotic dancer
claim: A robotic honeybee dancer (RoboBee) in an observation hive drew dance-followers, and some followers were recruited toward the advertised location, but recruitment was weaker and less consistent than for natural waggle dances.
source_title: Dancing honey bee robot elicits dance-following and recruits foragers
authors: Landgraf T, Bierbach D, Kirbach A, Cusing R, Oertel M, Lehmann K, Greggers U, Menzel R, Rojas R
venue: arXiv preprint (1803.07126); builds on Michelsen et al. 1992 Behav Ecol Sociobiol mechanical-bee model

claim: Guppies were more likely to accept and follow an interactive robotic fish (RoboFish) when it had realistic eyes and moved in response to the live fish (closed-loop) rather than along fixed paths.
source_title: RoboFish: increased acceptance of interactive robotic fish with realistic eyes and natural motion patterns by live Trinidadian guppies
authors: Landgraf T, Bierbach D, Nguyen H, Muggelberg N, Romanczuk P, Krause J

species: Taeniopygia guttata (zebra finch), females and males, interacting with a vocal robot
claim: Zebra finches exchanging calls with a computer-controlled 'vocal robot' learned to time their calls predictively to avoid overlapping the robot's calls. This predictive turn-taking depends on the forebrain song system.
source_title: The forebrain song system mediates predictive call timing in female and male zebra finches
authors: Benichov JI, Benezra SE, Vallentin D, Globerson E, Long MA, Tchernichovski O

species: Taeniopygia guttata (zebra finch); HVC recordings and manipulation during call exchanges
claim: In zebra finches, inhibition within the premotor nucleus HVC controls when a bird calls back to a partner in turn-taking. Recordings and manipulation of HVC activity linked inhibitory interneuron activity to the timing of vocal replies.
source_title: Inhibition within a premotor circuit controls the timing of vocal turn-taking in zebra finches
authors: Benichov JI, Vallentin D

species: Pheugopedius euophrys (plain-tailed wren), male-female duetting pairs, field neurophysiology
claim: Neural recordings from both members of plain-tailed wren pairs singing duets in their natural habitat (Ecuadorian Andes) showed that auditory input from the partner modulates activity in each bird's premotor HVC. This coordinates the rapid alternation of syllables between partners.
source_title: Neurophysiological coordination of duet singing (see also Fortune et al. 2011 Science 334:666-670)
authors: Coleman MJ, Day NF, Rivera-Parra P, Fortune ES

species: Megaptera novaeangliae (humpback whale), one adult female, field interactive playback
claim: Playback of a recorded humpback 'whup/throp' contact call to a free-ranging female humpback whale ('Twain') in Southeast Alaska produced an extended exchange. The whale approached and gave about three dozen call responses over roughly 20 minutes, with timing that tracked the playback intervals.
source_title: Interactive bioacoustic playback as a tool for detecting and exploring nonhuman intelligence: 'conversing' with an Alaskan humpback whale
authors: McCowan B, Hubbard J, Walker L, Fournet M, Doyle L, et al.

species: Stenella frontalis (Atlantic spotted dolphin), wild, Bahamas (Wild Dolphin Project) with human divers
claim: CHAT (Cetacean Hearing Augmentation Telemetry) is an underwater wearable computer. Researchers use it with free-ranging Atlantic spotted dolphins to play synthetic whistles associated with objects and to detect in real time whether dolphins mimic those whistles, as a platform for two-way communication experiments.
source_title: An underwater wearable computer for two way human-dolphin communication experimentation
authors: Kohlsdorf D, Gilliland S, Presti P, Starner T, Herzing D
venue: ISWC 2013 (Proceedings of the International Symposium on Wearable Computers)

claim: Google, Georgia Tech and the Wild Dolphin Project announced DolphinGemma, a roughly 400M-parameter audio model trained on the Wild Dolphin Project's Atlantic spotted dolphin recordings. It uses SoundStream tokenization to predict likely next vocalization sounds and is intended to run on smartphones within the CHAT field system. The announcement contained no peer-reviewed evaluation of meaning.
source_title: DolphinGemma announcement (Google blog / press, April 2025)
authors: Google DeepMind/Google with Georgia Tech (Starner) and Wild Dolphin Project (Herzing)

claim: In a rat 'brain-to-brain interface', cortical activity recorded from an encoder rat performing a tactile or visual discrimination was delivered as intracortical microstimulation to a decoder rat. The decoder chose correctly above chance, with modest accuracy of roughly 60-70% against 50% chance, and the encoder was rewarded when the decoder was correct, closing a dyadic loop.
source_title: A brain-to-brain interface for real-time sharing of sensorimotor information
authors: Pais-Vieira M, Lebedev M, Kunicki C, Wang J, Nicolelis MAL

species: Human operators and anesthetized Sprague-Dawley rats
claim: A non-invasive brain-to-brain interface linked a human's EEG (steady-state visual evoked potentials expressing intent) to transcranial focused ultrasound over an anesthetized rat's motor cortex. It triggered rat tail movements with high reported accuracy (about 94%).
source_title: Non-invasive brain-to-brain interface (BBI): establishing functional links between two brains
authors: Yoo SS, Kim H, Filandrianos E, Taghados SJ, Park S

species: Drosophila melanogaster; male VNC connectome (MANC) plus behavioral activation
claim: Male Adult Nerve Cord (MANC) connectome analysis identified nested premotor circuits in the ventral nerve cord that generate pulse versus sine song. Some neurons are shared and some are specific to one song type, and optogenetic tests supported their roles.
source_title: Nested neural circuits generate distinct acoustic signals during Drosophila courtship
authors: Lillvis JL, Wang K, Shiozaki HM, Xu M, Stern DL, Dickson BJ

species: Drosophila melanogaster; females; EM reconstruction plus two-photon imaging with song playback
claim: Baker et al. (2022) combined FlyWire EM reconstruction with calcium imaging during song playback. Auditory neurons in the Drosophila central brain show a continuum of pulse and sine song preferences. Cell types with different preferences are highly interconnected in a non-hierarchical network. Each cell type's song responses can nonetheless be predicted from its synaptic inputs.
source_title: Neural network organization for courtship-song feature detection in Drosophila
authors: Baker CA, McKellar C, Pang R, Nern A, Dorkenwald S, Pacheco DA, Eckstein N, Funke J, Dickson BJ, Murthy M

species: Multi-taxa (birds, mammals, others); trained on bioacoustics plus speech and music text-audio pairs
claim: NatureLM-audio (Earth Species Project) is an audio-language foundation model for bioacoustics. It combines a BEATs audio encoder with a Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct backbone, answers natural-language questions about animal audio zero-shot, and reported state-of-the-art zero-shot classification of unseen species. Weights, code and benchmark data were released.
source_title: NatureLM-audio: an Audio-Language Foundation Model for Bioacoustics
authors: Robinson D, Miron M, Hagiwara M, Pietquin O

claim: BEANS-Zero is ESP's test-only zero-shot benchmark for audio-language models. It adds call-type prediction, life-stage classification, captioning and individual counting on top of species classification and detection.
source_title: EarthSpeciesProject/BEANS-Zero (Hugging Face dataset)
authors: Earth Species Project
venue: Hugging Face; introduced in the NatureLM-audio paper

species: Sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus), Eastern Caribbean (Dominica) social units
claim: Sperm whale codas have combinatorial structure: rhythm and tempo can each be discretised, and 'rubato' (fine inter-click-interval changes relative to preceding codas) and 'ornamentation' (extra clicks) vary with conversational context. The repertoire is nearly an order of magnitude larger in distinguishable codas than previously described. The authors call this a 'sperm whale phonetic alphabet'.
source_title: Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations
authors: Sharma P, Gero S, Payne R, Gruber DF, Rus D, Torralba A, Andreas J (Project CETI / MIT CSAIL)

claim: Sperm whale codas have discrete spectral categories: one-formant 'a-coda vowels' and two-formant 'i-coda vowels'. These are orthogonal to rhythm-based coda types, recur across individuals, are used in dialogues, and are argued to be actively controlled rather than artefacts of movement.
source_title: Vowel- and Diphthong-Like Spectral Patterns in Sperm Whale Codas
authors: Beguš G et al. (UC Berkeley / Project CETI)

claim: DolphinGemma (Google with the Wild Dolphin Project and Georgia Tech, April 2025) is a ~400M-parameter audio-in/audio-out model. It uses the SoundStream tokenizer, was trained on WDP recordings of Atlantic spotted dolphins collected since 1985, and predicts likely next sounds in a sequence. It is sized to run on Pixel phones in the field.
source_title: DolphinGemma: How Google AI is helping decode dolphin communication
authors: Google (with Wild Dolphin Project and Georgia Tech)

claim: The WDP/Georgia Tech CHAT system (Cetacean Hearing Augmentation Telemetry) tries two-way interaction by pairing synthetic whistles with objects dolphins like, hoping dolphins will mimic them to request the objects. DolphinGemma is meant to speed recognition of those whistles.
source_title: Google Introduces DolphinGemma to Support Dolphin Communication Research
authors: InfoQ (reporting on Google/WDP/Georgia Tech)

species: Common bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus), Sarasota Bay, Florida
claim: Signature whistles make up roughly half of wild Sarasota Bay bottlenose dolphin whistles. Among the remaining non-signature whistles, Sayigh et al. (2025 preprint) found stereotyped types shared across many individuals. In playbacks one type (NSW-A) elicited avoidance, suggesting an alarm function, and another (NSW-B) occurred in response to unexpected situations, suggesting a 'query' function. Both functions are preliminary.
source_title: First evidence for widespread sharing of stereotyped non-signature whistle types by wild dolphins
authors: Sayigh LS et al. (WHOI; Sarasota Dolphin Research Program)

species: Zebra finch (Taeniopygia guttata); grey parrot (Psittacus erithacus) for the lifetime award
claim: The 2026 Coller-Dolittle US$100,000 prize (Jeremy Coller Foundation and Tel Aviv University, announced 26 June 2026) went to Julie E. Elie (Theunissen Lab, UC Berkeley) for showing that zebra finches classify their calls by meaning more than by acoustics. Irene Pepperberg received a Lifetime Achievement Award for her grey parrot work.
source_title: Scientists win US$100,000 in 2026 Coller Dolittle prize for latest step forward in interspecies communication research
authors: Jeremy Coller Foundation

claim: Zebra finches trained in an operant button-press task to discriminate 11 call types made errors that tracked shared meaning rather than acoustic similarity. They confused acoustically very different long- and short-distance contact calls, but never confused a short contact call with an acoustically similar short alarm call.
source_title: Categorical and semantic perception of the meaning of call types in zebra finches
authors: Elie JE, Theunissen FE et al.

species: Tursiops truncatus; common nightingale (Luscinia megarhynchos); cuttlefish (Sepia sp.); common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus)
claim: The 2025 Coller-Dolittle finalists were Sayigh (WHOI, dolphins; the eventual winner), Vallentin and Clemens (nightingales, with an AI model that generates and analyses whistles for interactive exchanges), Cohen-Bodénès and Neri (cuttlefish arm-wave signs), and Omer and Oren (Hebrew University, marmosets).
source_title: Finalists announced for Coller Dolittle challenge to decode animal communication
authors: NCCR Evolving Language (reporting the Coller/TAU announcement)

claim: Marmosets use phee calls to label specific conspecifics. Machine-learning classifiers found receiver-specific call features in natural phee-call dialogues, and in real-time computer-playback experiments marmosets responded more accurately when a call was directed at them.
source_title: Vocal labeling of others by nonhuman primates
authors: Oren G, ..., Omer DY

claim: Jaakkola (Learning & Behavior; online 2024, issue 2025) argues that the Oren et al. marmoset data allow at least one alternative, non-naming explanation. Any reply by Oren/Omer needs its own citation.
source_title: Do marmosets really have names?
authors: Jaakkola K

species: African savanna elephant (Loxodonta africana), wild female-offspring groups, Kenya
claim: Wild African savanna elephants address one another with individually specific rumbles. Machine learning predicted the receiver from a call's acoustic structure (469 rumbles, Amboseli and Samburu/Buffalo Springs, 1986-2022), apparently without imitation of the receiver's own calls. In playbacks, elephants responded more strongly (calling back or approaching) to calls originally addressed to them.
source_title: African elephants address one another with individually specific name-like calls
authors: Pardo MA, Fristrup K, Lolchuragi DS, Poole JH, Granli P, Moss C, Douglas-Hamilton I, Wittemyer G

claim: Berthet et al. reported that every bonobo call type occurs in at least one compositional combination, and that three combinations show 'nontrivial' compositionality, where one call modifies the meaning of the other. They inferred meaning from contextual features using a multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) pipeline.
source_title: Extensive compositionality in the vocal system of bonobos
authors: Berthet M, Surbeck M, Townsend SW et al.

claim: A reanalysis found that the Berthet et al. (2025) MCA pipeline flagged significant call-context relationships in 34.5-84.3% of randomised datasets with no true association. A full permutation test that respects the data's dependence structure gave a non-significant result on the original data (Monte Carlo p = 0.2597).
source_title: Structure without semantics: no evidence for bonobo compositionality in Berthet et al. (2025)
authors: Authors not captured in search results

species: Western chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes verus), Taï National Park, Côte d'Ivoire
claim: Wild Tai chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes verus) produce at least 16 different two-call combinations, drawn from a corpus of more than 12,000 recorded calls. From associations with the observed context, the authors describe four ways a call's meaning changes in combination: adding meaning, narrowing/clarifying meaning, non-compositional creation of a new meaning, and order effects. The meanings are inferred from context without playback tests, so the semantic interpretations remain hypotheses.
source_title: Versatile use of chimpanzee call combinations promotes meaning expansion
authors: Girard-Buttoz C, ..., Crockford C

species: Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus), captive colony
claim: In Egyptian fruit BATS (not fruit flies) monitored around the clock with audio and video for months, machine learning on ~15,000 everyday social vocalizations recovered the emitter's identity, the behavioural context, the listener's response and, partly, the call's addressee.
source_title: Everyday bat vocalizations contain information about emitter, addressee, context, and behavior
authors: Prat Y, Taub M, Yovel Y

species: Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus), captive groups
claim: Wireless neural recordings in the frontal cortex of groups of freely communicating Egyptian fruit bats showed that neural activity represented the identity of the vocalizing group member. Vocalizations by bats in the same cluster produced more accurate identity coding and higher brain-to-brain synchrony across the group.
source_title: Cortical representation of group social communication in bats
authors: Rose MC, Styr B, Schmid TA, Elie JE, Yartsev MM

species: Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus), mixed-sex groups of 5-10 wild-caught bats
claim: Hippocampal CA1 neurons in freely behaving wild Egyptian fruit bats living as a group in a lab cave encode the identity and sex of other bats. The strength of identity coding depends on the other bat's sex, hierarchy rank and social affiliation.
source_title: Hippocampal coding of identity, sex, hierarchy, and affiliation in a social group of wild fruit bats
authors: Ray S, ..., Ulanovsky N (Weizmann Institute)

claim: Realistic zebra finch song (pitch, amplitude and timbre) can be synthesised directly from neural activity recorded in a premotor song nucleus. One method maps activity into a low-dimensional biomechanical model of the vocal organ, the syrinx.
source_title: Neurally driven synthesis of learned, complex vocalizations
authors: Arneodo EM, Chen S, Brown DE, Gilja V, Gentner TQ

species: Drosophila melanogaster (male courtship song); Mus musculus; Lonchura striata domestica
claim: DAS (Deep Audio Segmenter) uses a temporal-convolutional network to annotate acoustic signals sample by sample from raw audio. It was validated on Drosophila courtship song (pulse and sine), mouse ultrasonic vocalizations and Bengalese finch song.
source_title: Fast and accurate annotation of acoustic signals with deep neural networks
authors: Steinfath E, Palacios-Muñoz A, Rottschäfer JR, Yuezak D, Clemens J

species: Drosophila spp. (courtship song); general animal acoustics
claim: SongExplorer is a browser-based deep-learning workflow for discovering, annotating and segmenting animal acoustic signals, including substrate vibrations. It is more accurate than heuristic segmenters, about as accurate as two expert human annotators, and allows rapid detection of song types in new species and of new song types in well-studied ones.
source_title: SongExplorer: A deep learning workflow for discovery and segmentation of animal acoustic communication signals
authors: Arthur BJ, Ding Y, ..., Turaga SC, Stern DL (Janelia)

species: Rat and mouse (Rattus norvegicus, Mus musculus)
claim: DeepSqueak treats spectrograms as images and uses a Faster-RCNN object detector to automatically detect and classify rodent ultrasonic vocalizations at human quality.
source_title: DeepSqueak: a deep learning-based system for detection and analysis of ultrasonic vocalizations
authors: Coffey KR, Marx RG, Neumaier JF

claim: A GLM-HMM fit without supervision to male-female courtship tracking data found three latent internal states in male D. melanogaster. Each state maps sensory feedback cues (mainly from the female) to song choices (pulse, sine, no song) differently, and together they predict moment-to-moment song patterning. These are model states inferred from behaviour, not recorded neural activity. Optogenetic activation of a neuron pair previously described as song command neurons (likely pIP10; confirm in the full text) was sufficient to shift the male between states (causal manipulation).
source_title: Unsupervised identification of the internal states that shape natural behavior
authors: Calhoun AJ, Pillow JW, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster, females and males, head-fixed
claim: Whole-central-brain volumetric calcium imaging with cross-brain registration showed that auditory (song-like) stimuli evoke responses in 33 of 36 major central-brain regions of D. melanogaster, in both sexes. Most responses were tuned to courtship-song features, including in regions tied to other senses and to motor control.
source_title: Auditory activity is diverse and widespread throughout the central brain of Drosophila
authors: Pacheco DA, Thiberge SY, Pnevmatikakis E, Murthy M

claim: Imaged D. melanogaster auditory neurons show a continuum of preferences across courtship-song modes (pulse vs sine) and response timescales. Neurons with different preferences are highly interconnected in a network that lacks hierarchical structure, as shown by combining activity imaging with connectome anatomy.
source_title: Neural network organization for courtship-song feature detection in Drosophila
authors: Baker CA, McKellar C, Pang R, Nern A, Dorkenwald S, Pacheco DA, ..., Murthy M

claim: Modelling fly auditory neurons as a nonlinearly adaptive, accumulating population code predicted female locomotor responses to naturally variable courtship song better than linear-nonlinear models, although both fit the neural data.
source_title: Inferring neural population codes for Drosophila acoustic communication
authors: Pang R, Baker CA, Murthy M, Pillow J

claim: In male D. melanogaster, calcium imaging shows that vPN1 neurons respond preferentially to pulse song with long IPIs, and pC1 responses across IPIs closely match males' behavioural chaining response. Optogenetic activation of vPN1 or pC1 in solitary males elicits courtship behaviours. The 2026 male CNS connectome shows vPN1 is GABAergic, so its drive of pC1 is best explained by disinhibition via mAL (Track 02).
source_title: Central neural circuitry mediating courtship song perception in male Drosophila
authors: Zhou C, Franconville R, Vaughan AG, Robinett CC, Jayaraman V, Baker BS
venue: eLife (per memory; venue not shown in result)

claim: An expert Science Policy Forum argues that ML advances make decoding communication in whales, crows, bats and other animals increasingly feasible. It says sender, receiver and context information must be integrated to generate hypotheses, which then require experimental validation.
source_title: Using machine learning to decode animal communication
authors: Rutz C, Bronstein M, Raskin A, et al.

claim: An ethics analysis argues that ML-based animal translation projects are scientifically warranted but carry real risks to animal communities, and lists those risks so researchers can avoid them.
source_title: Can we talk to the animals? The ethics of using machine learning to decode animal communication
authors: Alcantara M, Andrews K

species: Mus musculus (males; activity-tagged during courtship USV production)
claim: In male mice, intersectionally labeled periaqueductal gray neurons that were transiently active during courtship USVs (PAG-USV neurons) are necessary for USVs: silencing them abolished USVs and impaired attraction of females. Activating them triggered USVs even without female cues.
source_title: A Specialized Neural Circuit Gates Social Vocalizations in the Mouse
authors: Tschida K, Michael V, Takatoh J, Han BX, Zhao S, Sakurai K, Mooney R, Wang F

claim: Ablating PAG-USV neurons blocks USV production in both male and female mice, but distress calls (squeaks) are still produced. So the PAG-USV neurons are not required for squeaks. The neurons that gate squeaks were not identified; they may be a separate PAG population or lie outside the PAG.
source_title: Midbrain neurons important for the production of mouse ultrasonic vocalizations are not required for distress calls
authors: Ziobro P, Woo Y, He Z, Tschida K

claim: In mouse nucleus retroambiguus (RAm), USV production is associated with broad Fos activation throughout RAm, while distress squeaks are associated with activation in a much smaller region. The two activation patterns are largely nonoverlapping. (The caudal location of the squeak-related region needs checking in the full text.)
source_title: Production of Mouse Ultrasonic Vocalizations and Distress Calls Is Associated with Different Patterns of Fos Expression in the Nucleus Retroambiguus
authors: Ziobro P, Zheng D-J, et al., Tschida K (corresponding)

claim: Excitatory, vocalization-specific laryngeal premotor neurons in the retroambiguus nucleus (RAmVOC) are necessary and sufficient for vocal-cord closure and USV production. How long they are activated sets syllable length. Inhibitory input from the preBötzinger complex lets the need to inhale override vocal-cord closure.
source_title: Brainstem control of vocalization and its coordination with respiration
authors: Park J et al., Wang F lab (author list not verified in search results)

claim: In male Alston's singing mice, orofacial motor cortex (OMC) is needed for the rapid, flexible vocal responses that support countersinging. Note structure largely survives OMC inactivation, which implies the notes are generated by downstream circuits (presumed subcortical, not identified in the study), with OMC modulating them.
source_title: Motor cortical control of vocal interaction in neotropical singing mice
authors: Okobi DE Jr, Banerjee A, Matheson AMM, Phelps SM, Long MA

claim: In socially interacting zebra finches, local inhibition in the premotor nucleus HVC precedes premotor activity linked to calling. Blocking inhibition in HVC makes call replies faster and impairs the birds' ability to avoid overlapping their partner.
source_title: Inhibition within a premotor circuit controls the timing of vocal turn-taking in zebra finches
authors: Benichov JI, Vallentin D

claim: In zebra finches, HVC neurons that project to RA (HVC(RA)) each fire one short burst of a few spikes (usually cited as about 6 ms) at a single precise time in the song motif. The bursts are repeatable across renditions and occur in sequence across the population. The authors propose that this ultra-sparse sequence acts as an explicit clock for song timing (activity-recorded; the timing role is the authors' interpretation).
source_title: An ultra-sparse code underlies the generation of neural sequences in a songbird
authors: Hahnloser RHR, Kozhevnikov AA, Fee MS

claim: Serial block-face EM of zebra finch HVC shows HVC(RA) axons target almost only inhibitory interneurons close to the soma. Farther from the soma they target mostly excitatory neurons, about half of which are other HVC(RA) cells. This supports a synaptic-chain-like sequence architecture.
source_title: EM connectomics reveals axonal target variation in a sequence-generating network
authors: Kornfeld J et al., Long MA, Denk W (author list from memory)

claim: In the field cricket Gryllus bimaculatus (female phonotaxis system), selectivity for the species-specific pulse period comes from a brain network of five identified neurons and six synaptic connections. A delay line is combined with a coincidence detector.
source_title: An auditory feature detection circuit for sound pattern recognition
authors: Schöneich S, Kostarakos K, Hedwig B

species: Gryllus bimaculatus (model generalized across cricket species)
claim: A computational model of the cricket delay-line/coincidence network, fit to recordings, reproduces neuronal and behavioral tuning in G. bimaculatus. With parameter changes alone it produces every known cricket recognition phenotype for pulse duration and pause.
source_title: A small, computationally flexible network produces the phenotypic diversity of song recognition in crickets
authors: Clemens J, Schöneich S, Kostarakos K, Hennig RM, Hedwig B

claim: In the Drosophila melanogaster brain, calcium imaging of many newly characterized auditory cell types (reported as more than 20; count not confirmed) shows a continuum of preferences between pulse and sine song. Connectome reconstruction shows these neurons are highly interconnected in a network without hierarchical structure (imaging plus connectome-wiring). The contrast with the cricket's compact feed-forward detector is an interpretive comparison, not a result of this paper.
source_title: Neural network organization for courtship-song feature detection in Drosophila
authors: Baker CA, Clemens J, et al., Murthy M

claim: Wireless electrophysiology from pairs of Egyptian fruit bats showed neural activity correlated between the two brains (frontal cortex) on timescales from seconds to hours. The correlation was strongest in high-frequency LFP (>30 Hz), tracked how much the bats interacted, and rose before interactions began.
source_title: Correlated Neural Activity across the Brains of Socially Interacting Bats
authors: Zhang W, Yartsev MM

claim: In groups of Egyptian fruit bats, single frontal-cortex neurons tell apart the vocalizations of specific individuals, and their activity is restructured across social contexts. Inter-brain correlation is absent during trained vocalizations.
source_title: Cortical representation of group social communication in bats
authors: Rose MC, Styr B, Schmid TA, Elie JE, Yartsev MM

claim: In an observer Egyptian fruit bat, a subpopulation of dorsal CA1 hippocampal neurons encodes the position of a demonstrator bat in allocentric coordinates (social place cells). About half of them also encode the observer's own position.
source_title: Social place-cells in the bat hippocampus
authors: Omer DB, Maimon SR, Las L, Ulanovsky N

claim: Two-photon calcium imaging in the inferior colliculus of awake big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus) found individual neurons selective for social calls or for navigation (echolocation) calls, allowing robust population decoding of call category. Category-selective neurons formed spatial clusters independent of the frequency map (tonotopy).
source_title: Spatially clustered neurons in the bat midbrain encode vocalization categories
authors: Lawlor J, Wohlgemuth MJ, Moss CF, Kuchibhotla KV

claim: In the bat Carollia perspicillata, auditory-cortex neurons show spike patterns that distinguish upcoming echolocation calls from communication calls several hundred ms before vocal onset. The same activity reflects the number of syllables in a communication sequence.
source_title: Neurons in the bat auditory cortex encode class and complexity of future vocalizations
authors: (author list not verified in search results)

claim: In captive marmosets, phee calls in natural pair exchanges carried acoustic features that predicted which individual was addressed, which the authors interpret as vocal labels. In playback via a computerized system, marmosets responded more consistently to calls directed at them. Family members used similar labels and shared acoustic features, suggesting learning. This is a single-lab result; the 'name' interpretation is debated and awaits replication.
source_title: Vocal labeling of others by nonhuman primates
authors: Oren G, ... Omer DB

claim: In marmosets, theta-band power rises in both frontal and auditory cortex shortly before a call starts. Increased directed signaling from frontal to auditory cortex predicts suppression of auditory cortex and the acoustic properties of the call that follows.
source_title: Frontal-auditory cortical interactions and sensory prediction during vocal production in marmoset monkeys
authors: (author list not verified in search results)

claim: In freely moving marmosets in natural conversational exchanges, model-based (GLM) analysis of frontal-cortex neurons found activity related to hearing calls, producing calls in different social contexts, and behavioral state. The functional clusters did not align with prefrontal versus premotor subfields, suggesting a distributed organization.
source_title: Representing the dynamics of natural marmoset vocal behaviors in frontal cortex
authors: (Miller lab; author list not verified)

claim: Male C. elegans are attracted to hermaphrodite ascaroside cues such as ascr#8 within a preferred concentration range, via the male-specific CEM neurons. Individual CEMs in the same worm give dissimilar, even opposite-sign calcium responses, and this diversity shapes the sex-specific preference. The exact hermaphrodite response and how complete the loss is after CEM removal should be checked in the full text.
source_title: Contrasting responses within a single neuron class enable sex-specific attraction in Caenorhabditis elegans
authors: Narayan A et al., Sternberg PW (author list from memory)

claim: NeuroPAL is a multicolor transgene that gives every C. elegans hermaphrodite neuron a stereotyped color code, so whole-brain calcium imaging can be matched to neuron identity (Yemini et al., Cell 2021). The statements that at least six labs have published NeuroPAL whole-brain datasets, and that a 2025 GCaMP+NeuroPAL strain (KDK94) improved stimulus responses, come from separate later studies that must be cited on their own.
source_title: NeuroPAL: A Multicolor Atlas for Whole-Brain Neuronal Identification in C. elegans
authors: Yemini E et al., Hobert O

claim: In the honeybee primary auditory center, identified interneurons (DL-Int-1, DL-Int-2 and bilateral DL-dSEG-LP) respond with distinct spiking patterns to waggle-dance-like vibration pulses applied to the antenna, forming at least two parallel pathways. Johnston's organ is tuned to about 250–300 Hz, the main frequency of dance vibrations.
source_title: Interneurons in the Honeybee Primary Auditory Center Responding to Waggle Dance-Like Vibration Pulses
authors: Ai H et al. (author list from memory)

claim: By tracking cuttlefish chromatophores at high resolution, the authors inferred the activity of chromatophore motor neurons from how chromatophores co-fluctuate, and from that the structure of higher control levels. The result is a statistical hierarchy of motor control and low-dimensional skin-pattern dynamics.
source_title: Elucidating the control and development of skin patterning in cuttlefish
authors: Reiter S, Hülsdunk P, Woo T, ..., Kaschube M, Laurent G

claim: In developing zebrafish, brain-wide activity mapping plus two-photon imaging found 21 activity hotspots and biological-motion-tuned neurons in a socially activated dorsal thalamic nucleus. These neurons encode the local acceleration of fish-like dot motion and ignore global or continuous motion. EM shows they receive tectal input and project to hypothalamic social areas. Ablating the tectum or dorsal thalamus impairs social attraction but not repulsion.
source_title: Visual recognition of social signals by a tectothalamic neural circuit
authors: Kappel JM, Förster D, Slangewal K, Shainer I, Svara F, Donovan JC, Sherman S, Januszewski M, Baier H, Larsch J

claim: A June 2025 bioRxiv preprint (Fish-X) reports a synapse-level EM reconstruction of the retina, brain and anterior spinal cord of a 6 dpf larval zebrafish (>176,000 cells, >25 million synapses). APEX2 labeling marks noradrenergic, dopaminergic, serotonergic, hypocretinergic and glycinergic neurons, and glutamatergic and GABAergic identities are inferred from morphology. It builds on earlier whole-brain ssEM (Hildebrand et al. 2017) and partial synapse-level reconstructions.
source_title: Multiplexed neuromodulatory-type-annotated whole-brain EM-reconstruction of larval zebrafish
authors: (preprint; author list not verified)

claim: The MICrONS consortium co-registered calcium imaging of about 75,000 neurons in mouse primary and higher visual cortex with an EM reconstruction of the same ~1 mm³ volume, containing more than 200,000 cells and about 0.5 billion synapses. The flagship Nature paper was published April 9, 2025.
source_title: Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex
authors: The MICrONS Consortium

species: Homo sapiens (surgical temporal cortex sample, single individual)
claim: The H01 dataset reconstructs about 1 mm³ of human temporal cortex taken during epilepsy surgery. It contains about 57,000 cells, about 150 million synapses and about 230 mm of blood vessels, totals 1.4 petabytes, and was imaged at about 4×4×33 nm. Findings include glia outnumbering neurons about 2:1, deep-layer excitatory neurons that can be grouped by dendritic orientation, and rare strong axonal connections with up to 50 synapses.
source_title: A petavoxel fragment of human cerebral cortex reconstructed at nanoscale resolution
authors: Shapson-Coe A et al., Lichtman JW, Jain V

claim: NIH's BRAIN CONNECTS program, launched in 2023 (about $150M, 11 projects over 5 years), includes an Allen Institute-led project. It aims to image up to 10 mm³ of the mouse cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loop at synaptic resolution using two 91-beam electron microscopes in parallel. That is about 10 times the MICrONS volume (claim-writer's arithmetic).
source_title: Projects launch to map brain connections in mouse and macaque
authors: Allen Institute (news)

claim: In Xenopus laevis, calls come from a sexually differentiated hindbrain vocal central pattern generator. It includes the premotor nucleus DTAM (dorsal tegmental area of the medulla) and the laryngeal motor nucleus n.IX-X, which is generally regarded as homologous to the mammalian nucleus ambiguus. Sex-typical fictive vocalizations can be evoked in the isolated brain by applying serotonin or by electrically stimulating a premotor nucleus.
source_title: Xenopus Vocalizations Are Controlled by a Sexually Differentiated Hindbrain Central Pattern Generator
authors: Rhodes HJ, Yu HJ, Yamaguchi A (author list from memory)

claim: Whole-brain activity mapping (TRAP2 genetic tagging plus c-Fos) in adult male mice during courtship USVs across two sessions found consistent, robust activation in the caudal periaqueductal gray. Activity in the rostral caudoputamen correlated with how many USVs were produced.
source_title: Whole-Brain Mapping of Neuronal Activity Associated with Vocal Socialization Behaviors in Adult Mice
authors: Luo S-X, Chen S-Y, Kuo H-Y, Liu F-C

claim: Forebrain-to-midbrain (to PAG) pathways in mice include some that promote and others that suppress vocalization. From memory: preoptic-area inhibitory neurons promote USVs by disinhibiting PAG-USV neurons, while amygdala-derived projections suppress them.
source_title: Circuit and synaptic organization of forebrain-to-midbrain pathways that promote and suppress vocalization
authors: Michael V et al., Tschida K, Mooney R (author list from memory)

claim: The FlyWire whole-brain connectome of one adult female D. melanogaster (FAFB EM volume; Dorkenwald et al.) is publicly released through CAVE (datastack 'flywire_fafb_public'). It has static materializations v630 (an earlier snapshot, used by Shiu et al.) and v783. Reported size is ~139,000 neurons and ~5x10^7 chemical synapses (counts not re-verified here).
source_title: Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain
authors: Dorkenwald S, Matsliah A, Sterling AR, et al.; FlyWire Consortium; Murthy M, Seung HS

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult females (FAFB and hemibrain individuals)
claim: Cross-matching FlyWire to the hemibrain gave about 8,400 annotated cell types. Cell-type-level connectivity was largely reproducible between the two female brains, but individual connections and some cell counts varied. A single connectome should therefore not be treated as the canonical wiring of any communication circuit.
source_title: Whole-brain annotation and multi-connectome cell typing of Drosophila
authors: Schlegel P, Yin Y, Bates AS, et al.; Jefferis GSXE

claim: The philshiu/Drosophila_brain_model repository is a leaky integrate-and-fire model of the whole FlyWire brain. It supports activation (Poisson spiking at a fixed rate) and silencing of neurons by FlyWire ID and outputs spike times and rates. Per the search summary, the repository now uses FlyWire public release v783 connectivity by default, with the v630 data (used in the paper) kept in data/archive/ for reproducing the figures.
source_title: philshiu/Drosophila_brain_model (GitHub repository accompanying Shiu et al. 2024)
authors: Shiu PK et al.

claim: A leaky integrate-and-fire model of the whole FlyWire brain predicted the neurons involved in taste-to-feeding (sugar/water) and mechanosensory grooming pathways. It used only connectivity plus neurotransmitter identity (with no fitted weights). A subset of predictions was confirmed by optogenetics and imaging. The paper did not validate the model for courtship communication.
source_title: A Drosophila computational brain model reveals sensorimotor processing
authors: Shiu PK, Sterne GR, Spiller N, et al.; Scott K

claim: The hemibrain connectome (Scheffer et al.; one adult female; reported ~25,000 neurons covering much of the central brain, count not re-verified) is served through neuPrint as 'hemibrain' (current version v1.2.1).
source_title: A connectome and analysis of the adult Drosophila central brain
authors: Scheffer LK, Xu CS, Januszewski M, et al.

species: Drosophila melanogaster (hemibrain, MANC, optic-lobe, male CNS datasets)
claim: neuPrint is a web-based connectome analysis service (neuprint.janelia.org) with a Python client (neuprint-python) that serves EM connectomes including hemibrain and MANC. Programmatic access needs a personal token, which you get by logging into the neuPrint web interface (Google sign-in not verified here).
source_title: neuPrint: an open access tool for EM connectomics
authors: Plaza SM, Clements J, Dolafi T, et al.

claim: The male adult nerve cord (MANC) connectome reconstructs the complete ventral nerve cord of one male (about 23,000 neurons). It systematically annotates descending, ascending, motor and premotor neurons, including the wing-motor systems used for song.
source_title: A connectome of the male Drosophila ventral nerve cord; Systematic annotation of a complete adult male Drosophila nerve cord connectome reveals principles of functional organisation
authors: Takemura S et al.; Marin EC et al.

claim: A complete, fully proofread male CNS connectome (brain plus nerve cord, 166,700 neurons, 11,710 neuron types, annotated for fruitless/doublesex expression) was published in Cell in September 2026 after a 2025 bioRxiv preprint. Comparing it with the female brain gave 8,069 isomorphic, 138 dimorphic, 289 male-specific and 71 female-specific types. Sex-specific and dimorphic neurons are concentrated in higher-order brain centres, and the sensory and motor periphery is largely isomorphic.
source_title: Sexual dimorphism in the complete connectome of the Drosophila male central nervous system
authors: Berg S, Beckett IR, Costa M, et al.; Janelia FlyEM / Cambridge (Jefferis lab) and collaborators

claim: A complete connectome of one male optic lobe gave a neuron inventory (tens of thousands of neurons, several hundred cell types). It is served on neuPrint as 'optic-lobe' and matched to genetic driver lines.
source_title: Connectome-driven neural inventory of a complete visual system
authors: Nern A, Loesche F, Takemura S, et al.

claim: The BANC is the first synapse-resolution connectome to unite the brain and ventral nerve cord in one EM volume, from one adult female D. melanogaster. It has about 160,000 neurons (158,262 in coverage of the Nature paper; take the synapse count from the paper), was proofread by researchers and citizen scientists, and is annotated for cell type, neurotransmitter, hemilineage and cross-dataset identity. The data are available via flywire.ai/CAVE.
source_title: Distributed control circuits across a brain-and-cord connectome
authors: Bates AS, Phelps JS, Kim M, et al.; Wilson RI, Lee WCA

claim: CAVE (Connectome Annotation Versioning Engine) provides versioned, timestamped 'materializations' of continuously proofread segmentations and annotations. Users reach it through the caveclient Python package with an auth token. FlyWire and BANC run on this infrastructure.
source_title: CAVE: Connectome Annotation Versioning Engine
authors: Dorkenwald S, Schneider-Mizell CM, Brittain D, et al.

claim: Virtual Fly Brain is a free web atlas you can browse without an account. Under the Drosophila Anatomy Ontology it integrates EM connectome neurons, light-microscopy driver-line images and literature-curated neuron types, with cross-dataset queries (Court et al. 2023, Frontiers in Physiology).
source_title: Virtual Fly Brain: an interactive atlas of the Drosophila nervous system
authors: Court R, Costa M, Pilgrim C, et al.

claim: NeuronBridge (Janelia) is a web service and Python API that matches EM-reconstructed neurons (at least the hemibrain v1.2.1; MANC coverage not verified here) to FlyLight Gen1 MCFO and split-GAL4 light-microscopy images by colour-depth morphology search. Researchers use it to find driver lines for cell types identified in the connectome.
source_title: NeuronBridge: an intuitive web application for neuronal morphology search across large data sets
authors: Clements J, Goina C, Hubbard PM, et al.

claim: Janelia FlyLight released a searchable resource of GAL4 driver expression patterns at single-neuron resolution (MultiColor FlpOut images) for matching neurons to driver lines. A companion split-GAL4 driver-line resource covers many identified cell types, with stocks distributed via the Bloomington Drosophila Stock Center.
source_title: A searchable image resource of Drosophila GAL4 driver expression patterns with single neuron resolution; A split-GAL4 driver line resource for Drosophila neuron types
authors: Meissner GW et al.; FlyLight Project Team

species: Drosophila melanogaster (courting pairs), mice, other animals
claim: SLEAP is an open-source deep-learning system for multi-animal pose tracking. It supports bottom-up and top-down models, trains from relatively few labelled frames, and was benchmarked on datasets that include interacting fruit fly pairs (courtship) and mice.
source_title: SLEAP: A deep learning system for multi-animal pose tracking
authors: Pereira TD, Tabris N, Matsliah A, et al.; Murthy M, Talmo lab

claim: DAS (Deep Audio Segmenter) is an open-source deep network that annotates acoustic signals, including fly pulse and sine song, bird song and rodent vocalisations. It is accurate and has latency low enough for closed-loop experiments.
source_title: Fast and accurate annotation of acoustic signals with deep neural networks
authors: Steinfath E, Palacios-Munoz A, Rottschäfer JR, Yuezak D, Clemens J

claim: A careful experimental and statistical re-evaluation found no evidence for the reported ~55-s rhythm in the inter-pulse interval of D. melanogaster courtship song. Earlier positive reports were attributed to data-analysis artefacts. The original authors dispute this.
source_title: Experimental and statistical reevaluation provides no evidence for Drosophila courtship song rhythms
authors: Stern DL, Clemens J, Coen P, Calhoun AJ, Hogenesch JB, Arthur BJ, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult males and females
claim: Pan-neuronal calcium imaging in head-fixed flies found that responses to auditory stimuli, including courtship-song components, are diverse and widespread across the central brain in both sexes, not confined to the canonical AMMC/wedge auditory pathway.
source_title: Auditory activity is diverse and widespread throughout the central brain of Drosophila
authors: Pacheco DA, Thiberge SY, Pnevmatikakis E, Murthy M

species: Drosophila melanogaster, adult females (pC1) and both sexes (pC2)
claim: Activating the pC1d/e subset of female pC1 neurons drives a minutes-long persistent internal state. That state modulates several behaviours in the presence of males: receptivity, responses to courtship song, aggression and male-like courtship. EM reconstruction shows strong recurrent connectivity between pC1d/e and Fruitless+ aIPg neurons (Deutsch et al. 2020, eLife). pC2 neurons are tuned to temporal features of one song mode in both sexes and drive sex-specific behaviours (Deutsch et al. 2019, Current Biology).
source_title: The neural basis for a persistent internal state in Drosophila females; Shared song detector neurons in Drosophila male and female brains drive sex-specific behaviors
authors: Deutsch D, Pacheco DA, Encarnacion-Rivera L, Pereira T, Fathy R, Clemens J, Girardin C, Calhoun A, Ireland E, Burke A, Dorkenwald S, Seung HS, Murthy M
venue: eLife (2020, persistent state); Current Biology (2020, song detectors)

claim: Earth Species Project released NatureLM-audio, an audio-language foundation model for bioacoustics, with open weights. It is evaluated on the BEANS-Zero benchmark for zero-shot tasks such as species classification, call-type detection and captioning. None of these tasks show semantic 'translation'.
source_title: NatureLM-audio: an Audio-Language Foundation Model for Bioacoustics
authors: Robinson D, Miron M, Hagiwara M, Pietquin O, et al. (Earth Species Project)

claim: BEANS (the Benchmark of Animal Sounds) standardises evaluation of ML models on public bioacoustic datasets, covering classification and detection tasks across birds, mammals, anurans and insects.
source_title: BEANS: The Benchmark of Animal Sounds
authors: Hagiwara M, Hoffman B, Liu JY, Cusimano M, Effenberger F, Zacarian K

species: Sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus), Eastern Caribbean clans
claim: Analysis of a large Dominica Sperm Whale Project coda dataset found contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale codas, which the authors called a 'sperm whale phonetic alphabet' (rhythm, tempo, 'rubato', 'ornamentation'). The work shows structure, not meaning.
source_title: Contextual and combinatorial structure in sperm whale vocalisations
authors: Sharma P, Gero S, Payne R, Gruber DF, Rus D, Torralba A, Andreas J

claim: A Science Policy Forum argued that machine learning could help decode animal communication but warned that playing back AI-generated signals to wild animals risks disrupting behaviour and animal cultures. It called for ethical guidelines before any such interactive experiments.
source_title: Using machine learning to decode animal communication
authors: Rutz C, Bronstein M, Raskin A, Vernes SC, Zacarian K, Blasi DE

claim: Yovel and Rechavi frame two-way animal communication as 'the Doctor Dolittle challenge' and name three main obstacles. Per the search summary, meeting the challenge requires an AI model to use the animal's own signals, without the animal having to learn new signals, and to use them across many behavioural contexts, not only courtship or threat.
source_title: AI and the Doctor Dolittle challenge
authors: Yovel Y, Rechavi O

claim: The UK Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022 recognises all vertebrates, cephalopod molluscs and decapod crustaceans as sentient for policy purposes and creates an Animal Sentience Committee. Insects are not included.
source_title: Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022
authors: UK Parliament

claim: The DEFRA-commissioned LSE review (Birch et al. 2021) applied eight sentience criteria. It found very strong evidence in octopods, strong evidence in true crabs, and substantial evidence in other cephalopod and decapod groups. Evidence was weaker for some groups, such as shrimps and nautiloids, mainly for lack of research. It recommended treating all cephalopod molluscs and decapod crustaceans as sentient under UK animal welfare law.
source_title: Review of the Evidence of Sentience in Cephalopod Molluscs and Decapod Crustaceans
authors: Birch J, Burn C, Schnell A, Browning H, Crump A

claim: The New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness states strong scientific support for conscious experience in mammals and birds. It says there is at least a realistic possibility of conscious experience in all vertebrates and many invertebrates, including at minimum cephalopods, decapod crustaceans and insects, and that it is irresponsible to ignore that possibility in welfare decisions.
source_title: The New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness
authors: Andrews K, Birch J, Sebo J, et al. (signatories)
venue: NYU conference 'The Emerging Science of Animal Consciousness'

claim: A systematic review applying eight pain-related criteria across insect orders found strong evidence of pain-relevant capacities in adult Diptera (flies) and Blattodea (cockroaches), and weaker or absent evidence in many other orders, largely because they have been studied less.
source_title: Can insects feel pain? A review of the neural and behavioural evidence
authors: Gibbons M, Crump A, Barrett M, Sarlak S, Birch J, Chittka L

claim: Playing back vibrational disturbance signals through vineyard trellis wires disrupted mating communication in the leafhopper Scaphoideus titanus, the vector of grapevine flavescence dorée. This led to field trials of 'vibrational mating disruption'.
source_title: Exploitation of insect vibrational signals reveals a new method of pest management
authors: Eriksson A, Anfora G, Lucchi A, et al.; Mazzoni V

claim: Sound lures that mimic female Aedes aegypti flight tones (about 484 Hz) passively capture male mosquitoes in traps. The study shows better male collection for surveillance; it did not test population control.
source_title: The siren's song: exploitation of female flight tones to passively capture male Aedes aegypti (Diptera: Culicidae)
authors: Johnson BJ, Ritchie SA

species: Rare and endangered species generally (e.g., reptiles)
claim: Scientists warned that publishing precise location data for rare species had enabled poachers and collectors. They urged withholding or obscuring such data.
source_title: Do not publish
authors: Lindenmayer D, Scheele B
